articles.body_html:
🌊 What is Dear Stranger?

I recently launched Dear Stranger (dearst.app) — a cozy, anonymous, collaborative pixel art web game.

The concept is inspired by the old tradition of casting a message in a bottle into the ocean:

  1. Cast a bottle: You start by drawing a few pixel strokes on a small canvas (or choose from 8 classic masterpieces like Van Gogh's Starry Night or Monet).
  2. Drift across the sea: Your bottle travels across the world to strangers.
  3. Collaborate: 2 to 4 strangers take turns painting their fair share.
  4. Returns home: Once complete, the bottle journeys back to everyone who participated, complete with a celebratory replay of each painter's strokes and a travel map showing the countries it sailed through!

Play it directly in your browser (no sign-up required):
👉 https://dearst.app

🛠️ The Tech Stack: Exactly 0 npm dependencies

As web developers in 2026, our node_modules folders often weigh hundreds of megabytes just to render a button. For Dear Stranger, I set a personal challenge:

Can we build a full-featured, persistent, real-time multiplayer collaborative web app with ZERO external npm dependencies?

The answer is yes.

1. Pure Vanilla JS on the Frontend

  • Zero build tools: No Webpack, Vite, or Babel. Browsers have supported native ES modules for years.
  • HTML5 Canvas & SVG: Custom pixel manipulation, touch-enabled zooming/panning, and color palette sampling.
  • Dynamic Voyage Map: Natural Earth 1:50m geographic landmass rasterized into an ultra-compact dot grid rendered with pure SVG paths and beacons.

2. Node.js Built-in Standard Library on the Backend

  • Built on Node's native HTTP server and node:crypto.
  • Pure Web Push: RFC 8291 payload encryption and RFC 8292 VAPID signatures implemented purely with node:crypto — no web-push npm package required.
  • SQLite with WAL mode: Fast, zero-config persistent storage with foreign keys and immediate transactions.

3. Internationalization (i18n) from Day One

The game natively supports 5 languages:

  • 🇰🇷 Korean
  • 🇺🇸 English
  • 🇫🇷 French
  • 🇯🇵 Japanese
  • 🇨🇳 Chinese

Even the system NPC (Lighthouse · Keeper) and world country labels dynamically localize using the native Intl.DisplayNames API!

🎨 Game Design: Solving the "Trolling & Slacking" Problem

Collaborative art on the internet is notorious for two problems: trolls overwriting others' work and slackers drawing 1 pixel and dumping the rest on the next person.

Here is how Dear Stranger solves it through game mechanics:

  1. The 75% Fair Share Quota: Each painter receives an equal allocation of the remaining blank cells. You must fill at least 75% of your quota before the game lets you send the bottle onward.
  2. No Overwriting: Pixels already laid down by earlier strangers are immutable and locked.
  3. Report & Restoration (Kintsugi for pixels): If someone draws something offensive, any player can report that layer. The offender's layer is immediately hidden, and a blank space is created so another stranger can step in to restore the painting!

🖼️ What's next?

We launched with 8 classic museum masterpieces in both guided tracing mode and 64-pixel challenge mode. We plan to continuously add more classical artworks and community features.

Feel free to pick up a bottle, paint a few pixels, and see where your art travels:

🌊 Play the game: https://dearst.app

I’d love to hear your thoughts, feedback, and questions in the comments below!

articles.title: Angular Monorepos: When Does It Actually Make Sense?
articles.description: Angular applications rarely stay small forever.  A project starts with a single application, a few...
articles.body_html:
Angular applications rarely stay small forever.

A project starts with a single application, a few components, and some services. Over time, new requirements appear. Another application is introduced. Teams start sharing components, models, and utilities.

Eventually, someone suggests:

"We should move everything into a monorepo and use Nx."

And honestly, that might be a good idea.

But is it always necessary?

Angular CLI already supports multiple projects in a workspace. Nx adds powerful capabilities for dependency management, task execution, caching, and CI optimization, but those capabilities come with additional concepts and tooling.

So, when does Nx actually make sense?

Rather than simply explaining what a monorepo is, I want to explore this through a practical example, compare Angular CLI with Nx, and understand what changes when a workspace grows.

The goal isn't to prove that Nx is better.

The goal is to understand when the benefits of Nx justify its additional complexity.

1. First, What Problem Are We Trying to Solve?

Let's imagine a company with two Angular applications:

  • An administrative dashboard.
  • A customer portal.

Both applications display information about vehicles, appointments, and operational status.

Initially, they are completely independent.

company/
├── admin-app/
└── customer-app/

Each application has its own dependencies, configuration, and deployment pipeline.

This is a perfectly reasonable architecture.

However, the applications eventually start sharing code:

  • UI components.
  • Domain models.
  • API clients.
  • Validation utilities.
  • Design system elements.

Now we have a few options:

  1. Duplicate the code.
  2. Create an internal npm package.
  3. Share code through a monorepo.
  4. Introduce a workspace tool such as Nx.

The important distinction is that sharing code and sharing a repository are two different decisions.

A shared npm package can work perfectly well across separate repositories. A monorepo becomes particularly interesting when applications need to coordinate their dependencies, development, testing, and releases.

Before introducing a new tool, we should understand which problem we are actually solving.

2. Angular CLI Already Supports Monorepos

This is something that is sometimes overlooked.

Angular CLI is not limited to a single application per repository.

It supports workspaces containing multiple applications and libraries.

Let's create one.

Creating an Angular workspace 

ng new company-platform --no-create-application

cd company-platform

Now we can generate multiple applications:

ng generate application admin

ng generate application customer

And shared libraries:

ng generate library shared-ui

ng generate library shared-data

Our workspace now looks something like this:

company-platform/
├── projects/
│   ├── admin/
│   ├── customer/
│   ├── shared-ui/
│   └── shared-data/
├── angular.json
├── package.json
├── tsconfig.json
└── node_modules/

The exact generated files depend on the Angular version and project configuration, but the overall structure is familiar.

Angular CLI provides commands for building, testing, serving, and generating code across these projects.

For example:

ng serve admin

ng build customer

ng test admin

We can also build libraries:

ng build shared-ui

For many workspaces, this is already enough.

Sharing a component

Let's create a reusable vehicle card.

// projects/shared-ui/src/lib/vehicle-card/vehicle-card.component.ts

import { Component, input } from '@angular/core';

export interface Vehicle {
  id: string;
  registration: string;
  model: string;
}

@Component({
  selector: 'shared-vehicle-card',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    <article>
      <h3>{{ vehicle().registration }}</h3>
      <p>{{ vehicle().model }}</p>
    </article>
  `,
})
export class VehicleCardComponent {
  vehicle = input.required<Vehicle>();
}

We can export it from the library's public API:

// projects/shared-ui/src/public-api.ts

export * from './lib/vehicle-card/vehicle-card.component';

Then the admin application can import it:

import { Component } from '@angular/core';

import { VehicleCardComponent } from 'shared-ui';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-vehicle-list',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [VehicleCardComponent],
  template: `
    @for (vehicle of vehicles; track vehicle.id) {
      <shared-vehicle-card [vehicle]="vehicle" />
    }
  `,
})
export class VehicleListComponent {
  vehicles: Vehicle[] = [];
}

The customer application can use the same library.

This is a legitimate monorepo setup.

And we haven't needed Nx yet.

If your main requirement is simply sharing Angular libraries between a few applications, Angular CLI might already solve your problem.

3. What Changes When We Introduce Nx?

Nx doesn't replace Angular.

It builds on the Angular ecosystem and adds capabilities for managing larger workspaces.

According to the official Nx comparison, Angular CLI already supports application generation, libraries, building, testing, and local development.

Nx adds capabilities such as:

  • First-class monorepo tooling.
  • Project dependency graphs.
  • Enforced module boundaries.
  • Affected task execution.
  • Task orchestration.
  • Local task caching.
  • Remote caching.
  • Distributed task execution.

These are the differences worth exploring.

Creating an Nx workspace

We can create a new Angular workspace with Nx:

npx create-nx-workspace@latest company-platform \
  --template=nrwl/angular-template

The Angular template is available through Nx's workspace creation workflow.

Alternatively, we can migrate an existing Angular CLI workspace incrementally.

From the existing workspace:

npx nx add @nx/angular

This installs the Angular plugin and configures Nx integration.

It's important to keep Nx package versions compatible with each other. Using nx add is the recommended way to install the plugin into an existing Nx workspace.

Documentation:

  • Nx with Angular
  • Adding Nx to an existing workspace

Generating applications and libraries

With Nx, we can generate applications:

nx generate @nx/angular:app apps/admin

nx generate @nx/angular:app apps/customer

And libraries:

nx generate @nx/angular:lib libs/shared-ui

nx generate @nx/angular:lib libs/shared-data

Nx also supports more specific libraries:

nx generate @nx/angular:lib libs/vehicles/feature-list

nx generate @nx/angular:lib libs/vehicles/data-access

nx generate @nx/angular:lib libs/vehicles/ui

The exact generator options depend on the Nx and Angular versions, so check the Angular generator reference when building a real workspace.

A possible structure:

company-platform/
├── apps/
│   ├── admin/
│   └── customer/
│
├── libs/
│   ├── shared/
│   │   ├── ui/
│   │   └── data-access/
│   │
│   └── vehicles/
│       ├── feature-list/
│       ├── data-access/
│       └── ui/
│
├── nx.json
├── package.json
└── tsconfig.base.json

This organization makes it easier to understand which libraries belong to which domain.

However, the folder structure alone isn't the most important difference.

The real value starts when Nx understands the relationships between projects.

4. Project Graph: Understanding Dependencies

Imagine our workspace has these projects:

admin
customer
shared-ui
vehicles-data-access
billing
reports

The applications depend on shared libraries:

admin
 ├── shared-ui
 └── vehicles-data-access

customer
 ├── shared-ui
 └── vehicles-data-access

As the workspace grows, these relationships become increasingly important.

A change to shared-ui might affect both applications.

A change to billing might affect only the administrative application.

Without a clear understanding of these dependencies, it's easy to lose track of what needs to be tested or rebuilt.

Nx builds a project graph that represents relationships between projects.

You can inspect it with:

nx graph

The interactive graph helps developers understand how applications and libraries depend on each other.

This becomes especially useful when a workspace contains dozens or hundreds of projects.

Angular CLI can manage multiple projects, but it doesn't provide the same first-class project graph visualization and dependency-aware workflow as Nx.

The distinction isn't that Angular CLI cannot organize projects.

It's that Nx makes relationships between projects a central part of the development workflow.

5. Enforcing Architectural Boundaries

This is one of the most interesting features of Nx.

Let's say we have two applications:

apps/
├── admin/
└── customer/

And some shared libraries:

libs/
├── shared/
│   ├── ui/
│   └── utils/
│
└── vehicles/
    ├── feature-list/
    └── data-access/

A reasonable dependency structure might be:

admin → vehicles/feature-list
admin → shared/ui

customer → vehicles/feature-list
customer → shared/ui

vehicles/feature-list → vehicles/data-access

vehicles/data-access → shared/utils

But what happens when someone starts importing application-specific code into a shared library?

For example:

// libs/shared/ui/src/lib/admin-widget.ts

import { AdminService } from
  '../../../../apps/admin/src/app/services/admin.service';

This is a serious architectural problem.

A shared library should not depend on a specific application.

The problem isn't merely that the import path is ugly.

The dependency direction is wrong.

The shared library now depends on an application that depends on the shared library.

This can create circular dependencies, difficult refactoring, and unpredictable build relationships.

Nx module boundary rules

Nx provides the @nx/enforce-module-boundaries ESLint rule.

We can use project tags to describe architectural roles.

For example:

{
  "name": "admin",
  "tags": ["scope:admin", "type:app"]
}

A shared UI library:

{
  "name": "shared-ui",
  "tags": ["scope:shared", "type:ui"]
}

A vehicles data-access library:

{
  "name": "vehicles-data-access",
  "tags": ["scope:vehicles", "type:data-access"]
}

We can then define dependency constraints in ESLint.

A simplified configuration might look like this:

// eslint.config.mjs

import nx from '@nx/eslint-plugin';

export default [
  {
    files: ['**/*.ts'],
    rules: {
      '@nx/enforce-module-boundaries': [
        'error',
        {
          depConstraints: [
            {
              sourceTag: 'type:app',
              onlyDependOnLibsWithTags: [
                'type:app',
                'type:feature',
                'type:ui',
                'type:data-access',
                'type:util',
              ],
            },
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  },
];

This is an illustrative rule. A real workspace should define its constraints according to its architecture, and the exact ESLint configuration may vary with the Nx version and generated setup.

The important point is that Nx can help enforce architectural decisions instead of relying exclusively on code review.

This is a concrete benefit: Nx can help prevent certain dependency relationships from being introduced in the first place.

Angular CLI doesn't provide an equivalent first-class module-boundary enforcement feature.

6. The Performance Question: Is Nx Actually Faster?

This is where I think we need to be careful.

It's easy to find claims that Nx makes builds dramatically faster.

But performance depends on many factors:

  • Number of projects.
  • Number of dependencies.
  • Build configuration.
  • Test configuration.
  • Hardware.
  • CI environment.
  • Cache availability.
  • How much of the workspace changes.

A small Angular application might not see a meaningful improvement.

A large monorepo with many independent projects could benefit significantly.

Let's break down the relevant features.

6.1 Angular CLI already has caching

Before comparing Nx, we need to acknowledge something important.

Angular CLI already supports persistent disk caching.

For example:

ng build admin

Running the same build again can reuse cached work.

The cache is enabled by default for local development environments.

You can inspect its configuration:

ng cache info

And control it through the workspace configuration.

For example:

ng config cli.cache.environment all

Angular CLI cache documentation:

https://angular.dev/cli/cache

Therefore, it would be misleading to compare:

  • Angular CLI with caching disabled.
  • Nx with caching enabled.

That wouldn't be a fair comparison.

6.2 Nx adds task-level caching

Nx introduces caching at the task level.

A task might be:

nx build admin

Nx calculates a hash based on relevant inputs, including source files, dependencies, configuration, and other task inputs.

If the same task with the same relevant inputs has already completed, Nx can restore its cached outputs instead of executing the task again.

For example:

nx build admin

Run it again:

nx build admin

If the task is cacheable and its inputs haven't changed, Nx can restore the previous result.

This isn't simply caching Angular's compilation.

Nx can cache the results of different kinds of tasks, including builds, tests, linting, and other configured commands.

Documentation:

https://nx.dev/docs/features/cache-task-results

6.3 Running only affected projects

This is where Nx becomes particularly interesting.

Imagine a workspace with:

admin
customer
shared-ui
vehicles-data-access
billing
reports

A change to vehicles-data-access might affect:

vehicles-data-access
admin
customer

But it shouldn't necessarily require rebuilding:

billing
reports

Nx can determine which projects are affected by a change.

For example:

nx affected -t build

And:

nx affected -t test

These commands run the relevant tasks for affected projects.

This is particularly useful in CI, where running every build and test on every commit can become expensive.

The actual benefit depends on the dependency graph.

If every application depends on the same library, changing that library may affect nearly the entire workspace.

In that case, the number of skipped tasks will be smaller.

6.4 Parallel task execution

Nx can also run independent tasks in parallel.

For example:

nx run-many -t build

This runs build tasks across projects.

Nx's task graph determines which tasks can run concurrently and which depend on other tasks.

This can reduce total execution time when the workspace contains independent projects.

However, parallel execution also depends on available CPU and memory resources.

Running too many builds simultaneously can increase memory pressure and make the machine slower.

Parallelism is not automatically a performance improvement in every environment.

7. Remote Caching: A Different Kind of Benefit

Local caching is useful for individual developers.

Remote caching becomes particularly interesting for teams.

Imagine five developers working on the same workspace.

Developer A builds and tests a shared library.

Developer B later makes a change to an application that uses that library.

If the library's task inputs haven't changed, the previous result may be reusable.

Nx Cloud can share cache results between developers and CI environments.

This means the same task doesn't necessarily need to run repeatedly on every machine.

The workflow can look like this:

Developer A
    |
    | Build shared library
    v
Remote Cache
    |
    | Reuse result
    v
Developer B / CI

Nx Cloud documentation:

https://nx.dev/docs/features/ci-features/remote-cache

This can be valuable when:

  • Builds are expensive.
  • Many developers share the same workspace.
  • CI repeatedly executes similar tasks.
  • Projects have stable dependencies.

But remote caching introduces additional considerations:

  • Configuration.
  • Cache access and permissions.
  • Infrastructure or subscription costs, depending on the setup.
  • Correct task input and output configuration.

A cache is only useful when the system can safely determine that the previous result is valid.

8. Angular CLI vs Nx: A Practical Comparison

Let's summarize what we've discussed.

Capability Angular CLI Nx
Multiple Angular projects Yes Yes
Angular applications Yes Yes
Angular libraries Yes Yes
Shared components Yes Yes
Build, test, serve Yes Yes
Project dependency graph Limited compared with Nx First-class
Enforced module boundaries No equivalent built-in feature Yes
Affected project execution No equivalent first-class workflow Yes
Task-level caching Angular build cache Nx task cache
Remote caching Not built in Available through Nx Cloud
Distributed task execution Not built in Available through Nx Cloud
Additional tooling complexity Lower Higher

One detail matters here: Angular CLI and Nx are not mutually exclusive.

Nx integrates with Angular CLI builders and schematics.

You can continue using familiar Angular tooling while gradually introducing Nx features.

The official Nx comparison provides a more detailed overview.

9. Performance Benchmarks: Let's Measure Instead of Guessing

I think this is an important section to include in any serious comparison.

Rather than claiming that Nx is a certain percentage faster, we can create a reproducible benchmark.

Benchmark environment

Use a workspace with:

  • Two Angular applications.
  • Five shared libraries.
  • Unit tests for each application and library.
  • A production build configuration.
  • A fixed Node.js version.
  • A fixed Angular and Nx version.
  • The same machine and operating system.

Record the environment:

Operating System:
CPU:
RAM:
Node.js:
Package Manager:
Angular:
Nx:

Scenarios to measure

Scenario What we want to understand
Initial build Baseline execution time
Repeated build Cache effectiveness
Full workspace test Cost of running everything
Small application change Incremental build behavior
Shared library change Dependency impact
CI build Potential pipeline improvement
Remote cache hit Cross-machine reuse

Example benchmark commands

Angular CLI:

ng build admin
ng build customer

ng test admin
ng test customer

Nx:

nx build admin
nx build customer

nx test admin
nx test customer

Affected tasks:

nx affected -t build
nx affected -t test

For meaningful measurements, use the same workspace, equivalent build targets, and equivalent test coverage.

Important: Separate cold and warm runs

A cold run measures execution without reusable task results.

A warm run measures what happens when caches are available.

These are different scenarios and should not be mixed.

For each scenario:

  1. Run the task once.
  2. Record the initial execution.
  3. Run it again without changing inputs.
  4. Record the repeated execution.
  5. Repeat the experiment several times.
  6. Compare medians rather than relying on a single run.

For Nx, record whether the result came from:

  • Task execution.
  • Local cache.
  • Remote cache.

For Angular CLI, record the cache configuration and whether it was enabled.

Benchmark results template

Here is a table that could be included in the final article:

Scenario Angular CLI Nx Notes
Initial build TBD TBD Cold run
Repeated build TBD TBD Warm cache
Full test suite TBD TBD All projects
Small app change TBD TBD Incremental
Shared library change TBD TBD Affected projects
CI execution TBD TBD Pipeline comparison

I would only publish actual numbers after running the experiment.

If Nx is 20% faster in one scenario but only 3% faster in another, that's a much more interesting result than claiming it is universally faster.

It also makes the article more trustworthy.

10. When Does Nx Actually Make Sense?

Let's move away from features and focus on decisions.

Scenario 1: One Angular application 

my-app/
├── src/
├── angular.json
└── package.json

Nx probably isn't necessary.

Angular CLI provides everything required to develop, test, and build the application.

Introducing Nx might add concepts without solving a meaningful problem.

Scenario 2: Two independent applications 

company/
├── admin/
└── customer/

If these applications have:

  • Independent teams.
  • Independent releases.
  • Few shared dependencies.
  • Different lifecycles.

Separate repositories might be more appropriate.

A monorepo isn't automatically better simply because the applications belong to the same company.

Scenario 3: Multiple applications sharing a design system 

company-platform/
├── apps/
│   ├── admin/
│   └── customer/
│
└── libs/
    └── shared-ui/

This is a reasonable monorepo candidate.

Angular CLI can support this structure.

Nx becomes more attractive if we need:

  • Architectural dependency rules.
  • Project graph visualization.
  • Selective builds and tests.
  • Better task orchestration.
  • Remote caching.

Scenario 4: A large workspace with many domains 

company-platform/
├── apps/
│   ├── admin/
│   ├── customer/
│   └── operations/
│
└── libs/
    ├── vehicles/
    ├── appointments/
    ├── billing/
    ├── authentication/
    └── shared/

At this point, Nx can provide meaningful value.

The workspace needs more than a place to store projects.

It needs a way to understand dependencies, enforce architectural boundaries, and avoid unnecessary work.

Scenario 5: Microfrontends

Microfrontends introduce a different set of concerns.

Applications may share a repository but still need:

  • Independent deployment.
  • Independent ownership.
  • Runtime integration.
  • Separate release cycles.

A monorepo can support this arrangement, but it doesn't automatically solve microfrontend architecture.

Nx may help with workspace organization and CI, but deployment independence and runtime integration still require their own design.

11. A Practical Decision Checklist

Before adopting Nx, I would ask:

  • Do we have multiple applications or libraries that genuinely belong together?
  • Are dependencies between projects becoming difficult to understand?
  • Do we need architectural boundaries enforced automatically?
  • Are CI builds and tests executing unnecessary tasks?
  • Would task caching make a measurable difference?
  • Do we need to coordinate changes across applications?
  • Are the benefits worth introducing another tool into the development workflow?

If most answers are no, Angular CLI might be enough.

If several answers are yes, Nx deserves serious consideration.

The important part is not the number of applications.

It's the complexity of coordinating them.

12. My Take: Start Simple, Introduce Nx When the Problems Become Real

I don't think Nx should be the default answer to every Angular workspace.

Angular CLI is capable of managing multiple applications and libraries.

For smaller workspaces, that may be all you need.

But as a workspace grows, the problems change.

The challenge is no longer just creating applications or sharing components.

It becomes:

  • Understanding dependencies.
  • Enforcing architectural boundaries.
  • Avoiding unnecessary builds.
  • Coordinating tasks.
  • Improving CI performance.
  • Maintaining a consistent development workflow.

This is where Nx becomes valuable.

Not because it makes your architecture automatically better.

Not because every monorepo needs it.

But because it provides tooling for problems that become increasingly difficult to manage manually.

And that's the distinction I think matters most.

Don't introduce Nx because your project has multiple applications. Introduce it when the complexity of managing those applications becomes a problem that Nx can actually solve.

Final Thoughts

Monorepos are a strategy, not an architectural achievement.

Angular CLI already provides a solid foundation for organizing multiple applications and libraries.

Nx extends that foundation with project graphs, dependency constraints, task orchestration, caching, and CI optimization.

Those features can make a significant difference in larger workspaces.

But they also introduce additional concepts and configuration.

The best choice depends on the problems your team is facing today, not the scale you imagine your project might eventually reach.

I'd rather start with a simple workspace and introduce complexity when it becomes useful than build a sophisticated monorepo that solves problems we don't have.

What About Your Projects?

Have you adopted Nx in an Angular workspace?

Did it actually improve your development experience or CI performance?

Or did Angular CLI turn out to be enough?

I'm particularly interested in real-world experiences with affected builds, caching, and architectural boundaries.

articles.title: Desktops have SQLite. Servers have Postgres. Now, the browser finally has WebDB — Introducing WebDB
articles.description: How the pain of IndexedDB and bloated WASM ports led me to build a ~19KB browser-native relational database engine.
articles.body_html:
Stop shipping multi-megabyte desktop databases to the browser—the Web finally has its own DB.

If you’ve ever built an offline-first or local-first web application, you already know the storage struggle. Everything starts out fine when you're just caching a few JSON objects. Then, real product requirements kick in: you need to join orders with customers, filter by multiple conditions, calculate totals, paginate results, and keep two open browser tabs in sync without corrupting data.

At that point, you have two choices—and both hurt.

Option 1: The IndexedDB Boilerplate Trap

You start with raw IndexedDB (or a thin wrapper around it). Pretty quickly, you realize IndexedDB isn't a relational database. Want to join two tables? You’re writing manual JavaScript loops and merging cursors in memory. Want a compound filter with sorting and pagination? You’re fighting key ranges and writing dozens of lines of imperative code for what should have been a 3-line query.

Option 2: The Heavy Desktop WASM Port

Frustrated with IndexedDB, you reach for SQLite WASM or PGlite. Now you have real relational queries, which feels great—until you look at the trade-offs:

  1. Massive bundles: You're shipping a 1 MB to 5 MB+ WebAssembly binary designed for desktop filesystems just to store data in a browser tab.
  2. Server header headaches: To get fast synchronous file access in a Worker, you need SharedArrayBuffer, which forces you to add strict COOP and COEP isolation headers to your server—instantly breaking third-party scripts, embeds, and auth popups.
  3. Wasted CPU cycles: Your JavaScript code builds a query, serializes it into a SQL text string, crosses the WASM boundary, and hands it to a multi-megabyte C SQL lexer and AST parser just to tokenize that string back into bytecode instructions.

After hitting this wall one too many times while building offline-capable apps, I asked a simple question: What if we built a relational database engine natively for the browser from scratch?

Today, I’m really excited to launch WebDB.

Rethinking the Architecture: Direct-to-Bytecode

Desktop databases need a SQL text parser because queries come over a network socket as raw strings. In the browser, your application code and your database live in the exact same runtime. Why are we serializing objects into strings just to parse them back again?

WebDB eliminates the middleman entirely:

  • Legacy WASM Ports (4 Stages): JS Query / ORM ➔ SQL String Serialization ➔ C SQL Lexer & AST Parser (+1.5 MB bloat) ➔ WASM Execution
  • WebDB (2 Stages): Fluent TypeScript Query Builder ➔ Direct VDBE Binary Bytecode (< 0.05ms)

Because WebDB compiles fluent TypeScript AST directly into compact binary opcodes (OP_INDEX_SCAN, OP_RESULT_ROW, etc.), we don't need to bundle a massive C string parser.

The result? A full relational engine—with B+Tree indexes, joins, aggregates, subqueries, and crash-proof ACID transactions—inside a ~19 KB gzipped WebAssembly core (~51 KB raw), with a pure JS fallback included.

What Makes WebDB Different?

  • ~19 KB Gzipped WASM Core: Around 95% smaller than typical desktop SQLite or Postgres WASM ports.
  • Up to 8.7x Faster than Official SQLite WASM: Skipping SQL string parsing and Emscripten Asyncify stack-unwinding makes in-memory and indexed workloads significantly faster.
  • Zero COOP/COEP Server Headers: Works out of the box on any static host or CDN without breaking your page isolation.
  • Native Async Virtual File System (VFS): Suspends cleanly on 4 KB page faults over OPFS and IndexedDB. You can even query multi-gigabyte read-only databases hosted on S3 or a CDN via HTTP Range: bytes=X-Y requests without downloading the whole file.
  • Crash-Proof ACID & WAL: Write-Ahead Logging with IEEE 802.3 CRC32 checksums on every 4 KB page prevents corruption when users suddenly close a tab. Multi-tab readers and writers coordinate automatically via navigator.locks.
  • 16-Byte Binary UUIDv7 & ULID: Packs UUIDs into 16 raw bytes (58% smaller than 36-char strings) for fast, zero-fragmentation B+Tree inserts.

How to Use WebDB

1. Define a Schema & Run Relational Queries

No SQL strings to escape. You get full TypeScript autocompletion for schemas, composite B+Tree indexes, JOINs, GROUP BY, HAVING, and aggregates:

// 1. Define relational schema with typed binary columns & B+Tree indexes
await db.createTable("orders", [
  { name: "id", type: "UUID", primaryKey: true }, // Packed into 16 raw bytes
  { name: "customer_id", type: "UUID", notNull: true },
  { name: "status", type: "TEXT", notNull: true },
  { name: "total", type: "FLOAT64", notNull: true },
]);

await db.createIndex("orders", ["status", "total"]);

// 2. Fluent relational query with JOINs, aggregates & filtering
const topCustomers = await db
  .from("orders")
  .join("customers", "orders.customer_id", "=", "customers.id")
  .select("customers.name as customer")
  .sum("orders.total", "lifetimeValue")
  .count("*", "orderCount")
  .where("orders.status", "=", "paid")
  .groupBy("customers.name")
  .having("lifetimeValue", ">=", 500)
  .orderBy("lifetimeValue", "desc")
  .limit(10)
  .toArray();

If you ever want to see what the cost-based query planner is doing under the hood, just call .explain() on any query to inspect the generated VDBE bytecode instructions directly.

2. Reactive Live Queries (React, Vue, Angular & Plain JS)

One of the most annoying parts of offline apps is wiring manual event buses around database writes so your UI knows when to re-render.

WebDB ships with isolated framework subpaths (under 1 KB gzipped each) that automatically inspect your query AST—including JOINs and subqueries. When a relevant table mutates in the current tab, a Web Worker, or another open browser tab (via BroadcastChannel), your UI updates automatically:

import { useLiveQuery } from "@ahmadmoussawi/webdb/react";

export function OrderDashboard({ status }: { status: string }) {
  // Automatically tracks 'orders' AND joined 'customers' table!
  const { data: orders, isLoading } = useLiveQuery(
    () =>
      db
        .from("orders")
        .join("customers", "orders.customer_id", "=", "customers.id")
        .where("orders.status", "=", status)
        .orderBy("orders.id", "desc"),
    [status],
    { initialData: [] }
  );

  // Mutating 'orders' (here or in another tab) automatically updates the UI!
  const markPaid = (id: string) =>
    db.from("orders").where("id", "=", id).update({ status: "paid" });

  if (isLoading) return <p>Loading live orders...</p>;
  return <OrderTable rows={orders} onMarkPaid={markPaid} />;
}

Performance Benchmarks (5,000 Rows In-Memory)

Because WebDB compiles TypeScript directly into binary opcodes and avoids C parser overhead, both the ~19 KB WASM engine and even the pure JS fallback beat official SQLite WASM (:memory:) across common relational workloads (tested on a MacBook Pro M1 Max):

Workload Scenario WebDB (WASM) WebDB (Pure JS) SQLite WASM Speedup vs SQLite
Range Filter Scan 1,091.7 ops/s 444.0 ops/s 125.9 ops/s 8.7x faster
Bulk Batch Insert 359,152 ops/s 301,932 ops/s 156,576 ops/s 2.3x faster
Batch Point Lookups 334,448 ops/s 234,192 ops/s 148,148 ops/s 2.3x faster
Indexed 2-Table JOIN 755.3 ops/s 494.6 ops/s 440.1 ops/s 1.7x faster
Filter + Sort + Limit 2,381.0 ops/s 681.7 ops/s 1,483.7 ops/s 1.6x faster

Don't just take my numbers for it—you can run the live benchmark suite on your own machine here.

Try It in Your Browser (Studio IDE)

To make debugging local databases easier, I also built the WebDB Studio Playground.

Right in your browser, you can write queries with full autocompletion, inspect raw binary 4 KB slotted pages in real time, visualize B+Tree structures, and even share live compressed .webdb.gz databases via URL.

Links & Resources

WebDB is completely open-source under the MIT license. If you’ve ever felt the friction of building offline-first or local-first web apps, I’d love for you to try it out, break it, and let me know what you think!

  • Website & Documentation: https://webdb.dev/
  • Live Studio IDE Playground: https://webdb.dev/playground/
  • In-Browser Benchmarks: https://webdb.dev/benchmark/
  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/ahmad-moussawi/webdb (If you find it useful, a ⭐ on GitHub helps a ton!)

What's been your biggest headache when dealing with client-side storage in the browser? Let me know in the comments!

articles.title: Folio.AspNetCore — an embeddable OpenAPI UI for ASP.NET Core
articles.description: Most OpenAPI UIs for ASP.NET Core work the same way: you generate a spec, then host a separate set of...
articles.body_html:
Most OpenAPI UIs for ASP.NET Core work the same way: you generate a spec,
then host a separate set of static files to render it. That's fine until
you want it to just... work, out of the box, offline, without another
build step in your pipeline.

I spent the last few months building Folio.AspNetCore — an OpenAPI
documentation and testing UI that ships entirely as a NuGet package. No
static files to host yourself, no CDN dependencies, no separate build
step. Install the package, point it at your OpenAPI document, done.

dotnet add package Folio.AspNetCore

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddOpenApi();

var app = builder.Build();
app.MapOpenApi();

app.UseFolio(options =>
{
    options.SpecUrl = "/openapi/v1.json";
});

app.Run();

That's the whole setup. Open /folio and you get the full UI.

What you get

Browsing

  • Endpoint list, grouped and searchable, generated straight from the spec
  • A full, separately-browsable model/schema catalog — not just inline types buried in each endpoint
  • Markdown-rendered descriptions (from the spec's own description fields)

A real request builder, not a raw JSON textarea

Parameters and request body fields get the right control for their
schema type — text inputs, number steppers, boolean toggles, enum
dropdowns, date pickers, nested object/array editors. You can still drop
into raw JSON if you want to.

Live code generation, in six languages

Every request gets an equivalent code snippet — cURL, JavaScript
(fetch), Python (requests), C# (HttpClient), Go (net/http),
PowerShell (Invoke-RestMethod) — updated live as you fill in the form,
before you even hit Send. Syntax-highlighted too.

Per-endpoint role visibility

If your endpoints use [Authorize(Roles = "...")], Folio shows exactly
which roles are required, right in the sidebar and on the endpoint page —
read directly from your routing metadata via EndpointDataSource.
Nothing to configure, nothing duplicated: it's a live mirror of what your
code already declares.

app.MapPost("/api/items", CreateItem)
    .RequireAuthorization(new AuthorizeAttribute { Roles = "Admin" });

That attribute alone is enough — Folio picks it up automatically.

Environments, headers, auth

  • Switch between base URLs (local/staging/prod) without touching code, or import servers[] straight from the spec
  • Global headers (e.g. an API key) applied to every request, separate from per-endpoint headers
  • A dedicated modal for the spec's own security schemes (apiKey, HTTP Bearer/Basic)

Gating the docs themselves

Two ways to put a login in front of the UI:

// Integrate with auth you already have
app.UseFolio(options =>
{
    options.AuthorizationPolicy = "FolioAccess";
    options.LogoutUrl = "/account/logout";
});

// Or a self-contained cookie-based login, zero existing auth required
builder.Services.AddFolioAuth(options =>
{
    options.Users = builder.Configuration.GetSection("Users").Get<List<FolioUser>>() ?? [];
});

app.UseFolioAuth();
app.UseFolio(options => options.SpecUrl = "/openapi/v1.json");

Fine-grained control over what's shown

Every major UI element — the execute button, code generator, role
badges, schema viewer, environment switcher, and more — can be toggled
independently:

app.UseFolio(options =>
{
    options.ShowTryItOut = false; // read-only docs deployment, say
});

...or bound from appsettings.json explicitly (Folio never reads config
on its own — this only runs if you call it):

app.UseFolio((context, options) =>
{
    options.ReadFrom.Configuration(context.Configuration, "Folio");
});

How it's built

It's a classic ASP.NET Core middleware (app.Use...), not endpoint
routing. The UI's HTML/CSS/JS live as embedded resources, served through
a real StaticFileMiddleware on top of ManifestEmbeddedFileProvider —
proper ETag/Last-Modified/conditional requests, not hand-rolled file
serving.

Multi-targets .NET 6 through 9.

Try it 

dotnet add package Folio.AspNetCore
  • GitHub: https://github.com/bekov0004/Folio.AspNetCore
  • NuGet: https://www.nuget.org/packages/Folio.AspNetCore
  • Wiki (getting started, auth setup, FAQ): https://github.com/bekov0004/Folio.AspNetCore/wiki

Feedback and issues welcome — especially if something's missing for your
use case.

articles.title: I built an open-source AI interface builder that exports to React, Vue, Svelte… and Roblox
articles.description: Drag components onto a canvas, ask any AI model to build pages, and export to HTML, React, Vue, Svelte, Roblox Luau or LÖVE. Free and MIT-licensed.
articles.body_html:
Hey DEV 👋

I've been building openconstructor: a browser-based interface builder where you put together pages from ready-made blocks and an AI assistant. It's free, needs no install, and the whole thing is open source under MIT.

👉 Try it: https://openconstructor.pw
👉 Source: https://github.com/Kuloka/openconstructor

What it does

1. A real component library. There are 145 components in 12 sections: AI & Chat (chat windows, prompt composers, "thinking" indicators, agent steps), Dashboards and charts, Pricing & Commerce, Auth, Navigation, Landing sections, Effects and more. Each one is plain HTML + CSS with no framework lock-in. Animated components play when you hover them in the catalog. Browse the sections →

2. Bring your own AI. Connect a key from OpenRouter, Google Gemini, Groq, Cerebras, Mistral, DeepSeek, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI or Together, then type "a pricing section with three plans". The block lands on the canvas. Select an element first and only that element gets changed.
Your keys stay in your browser and are sent only to the provider you picked. On a budget? Groq's no-cost plan with GPT-OSS 120B and Gemini Flash both work well. More on the AI generator →

3. Screenshot → blocks. Paste a screenshot of any site or mockup (Ctrl+V works) and a vision model rebuilds it as editable HTML/CSS.

4. Edit without code. Double-click an element to edit its text directly on the page. Click any part of it to change color, size, weight, radius or padding in a small inspector.

5. ⚗ Fusion. This is the experiment I'm most curious about. Right-click a component → fuse with… → click another one. The AI breeds a new component that does the first one's job in the second one's visual style. A sign-in form × a glassmorphism card gives you a glass sign-in form, in its own new design rather than a copy of either.

6. Responsive by default (if you want). Switch the page from free layout to stack. Blocks then flow top to bottom, and the export adapts to any screen. A preview shows the page on phone, tablet and desktop side by side.

7. Page-wide themes. One click recolors every component on the page to a new accent. Grays stay gray, and alpha and notation are preserved. You can also swap any single color everywhere, or set one font and one corner style for the whole page.

Export anywhere, including game engines

This is the part I haven't seen in other web builders:

  • HTML: one self-contained file
  • React / Vue / Svelte: a ready component file
  • Roblox (Luau): a LocalScript that builds your UI with ScreenGui, Frame, TextLabel, TextButton, UICorner, UIStroke, UIGradient and a UIScale that fits any screen. Drop it into StarterPlayerScripts and press Play. How it works →
  • LÖVE 2D (Lua): a main.lua that draws the layout with love.graphics. Details →
  • Flutter, SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose, Tailwind: AI-assisted ports, a starting point to review.

The Roblox and LÖVE exports don't guess from your HTML. They read the rendered layout, using each element's real position, size, colors, radius, borders and text, and then generate native UI code from that snapshot. To be clear, they're visual only: buttons and text boxes have no logic wired up yet.

Share it

Hit publish and the page gets a public link like openconstructor.pw/p/my-page. Signed-in users can also keep projects in the cloud and open them on any device. Sign-in is optional, and everything else works without an account.

How it's built

  • Vite + vanilla JS for the editor. React 19 only for the landing page and the chat input.
  • Every element renders in its own sandboxed iframe with a strict CSP and no scripts. AI-generated code can't touch the editor or your keys.
  • Supabase for auth (Google, GitHub, email) and storage.
  • Cloudflare for hosting. A small Worker serves published pages, sandboxed with script-src 'none'.

What's next

I'd love feedback, especially on:

  • Which export target you'd actually use, and what's missing from it
  • Components you wish were in the library
  • Whether Fusion produces anything useful for you, or just chaos 😄

Issues and PRs are very welcome: https://github.com/Kuloka/openconstructor

If you like the project, a ⭐ on GitHub really helps a solo dev get it in front of more people. Thanks for reading!

articles.title: 10 AI Terms Every Developer Should Know to Build Better Systems
articles.description: In my last speech, I wanted the audience to leave with something they could use beyond a particular...
articles.body_html:
In my last speech, I wanted the audience to leave with something they could use beyond a particular AI tool.

So I focused on how to think with AI.

While building ReThynk AI, one lesson has become central to my thinking: start with the problem. Understand what needs to happen, who needs it, and how you will know whether your solution works.

Technical knowledge becomes valuable when it helps us answer those questions.

That is why I want developers to understand these ten terms. Each gives you a way to examine your application, identify a weakness, and make a better decision.

Let us connect them through one example: building an AI customer-support assistant.

1. Context window

The context window is the amount of information a model can work with during a response, measured in tokens. Its capacity must accommodate the relevant input and generated output, subject to the model’s limits. It is different from permanent memory.

Imagine your support assistant needs the customer’s question, conversation history, and refund policy. Those compete for space alongside instructions and tool results.

A larger window gives you more room. You still need to decide what deserves that room.

2. Context engineering

Context engineering means selecting, organizing, and maintaining the information available to the model as it works. This includes instructions, documents, conversation history, and tool results.

For our assistant, loading every policy document could introduce outdated or irrelevant information. Selecting the current policy for the customer’s region gives it a more useful starting point.

My question here is simple: Have I given the system what it needs to make this particular decision?

3. Embeddings

Embeddings represent information as numerical vectors. Suitable embedding models allow us to compare text by semantic similarity, which is useful for search, clustering, and retrieval.

A customer writes, “My parcel never arrived.” Your documentation calls this a “missing delivery.” Embedding-based search can help connect the two despite their different wording.

However, a similar document can still be the wrong document. You must also consider details such as product, region, and policy date.

4. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG

RAG retrieves relevant information and supplies it to a model to help generate an answer. It connects generation with external sources such as documents or databases.

Our assistant could retrieve a delivery policy before explaining the available options.

That sounds straightforward, but there are two questions to investigate: did retrieval find the right information, and did the model use it correctly?

Connecting a document store is the beginning of that work.

5. Tool calling

Tool calling allows a model to request an external function using structured arguments. For custom functions, your application executes the function and returns its result to the model.

For example, the assistant might request:

get_order_status(order_id="12345")

Your application must check whether the customer can access that order before executing the request.

The model can propose an action. Your software remains responsible for enforcing permissions and validating inputs.

6. Workflows and agents

In Anthropic’s architectural distinction, workflows follow predefined code paths, while agents dynamically direct their processes and tool use. Different products may use these labels differently, so the underlying behavior matters.

A support workflow might always check the order, retrieve the policy, and draft a response.

An agent might decide which investigation to perform next based on what it discovers.

When building, I would ask how much flexibility the problem requires. A predictable process can be easier to inspect, test, and maintain.

7. Model Context Protocol, or MCP

MCP standardizes how AI applications connect with capabilities exposed by servers, including tools, resources, and prompts. Its architecture separates the host application, clients, and servers.

For our support assistant, an MCP server could expose order-search tools or policy resources.

This helps define the connection. You still need to design access controls, tool behavior, and error handling.

Understanding the protocol should help you build clearer interfaces between your AI application and the systems it uses.

8. Evaluations, or evals

Evaluations are structured checks of how a system performs on representative tasks. For a RAG application, useful dimensions include correctness, relevance, completeness, and whether the response is supported by its supplied context.

Our assistant needs test cases for missing deliveries, conflicting policies, unavailable order data, and questions it cannot answer.

My Six Sigma background makes this especially meaningful to me. Before improving a process, we need a clear definition of acceptable performance.

A convincing demonstration gives us something to investigate. Evaluation gives us evidence across cases.

9. Observability

Observability helps us understand a system’s behavior through telemetry such as traces, metrics, and logs. A trace can follow a request through multiple operations.

Suppose our assistant gives a poor answer after taking fifteen seconds. We need to discover where the time went, which documents were retrieved, and whether a tool failed.

For AI applications, I would track the relevant retrieval, model, and tool steps while protecting sensitive customer information.

We can improve more effectively when we can locate the failure.

10. Idempotency

An idempotent operation can be repeated without producing additional effects beyond the intended first operation. This matters when requests are retried after timeouts or interrupted connections.

Imagine a refund succeeds, but the response never reaches the assistant. It retries.

The system should recognize the same logical refund request and avoid issuing another payment. Implementing that requires coordination with the service performing the action.

A retry is a small technical detail until it changes someone’s account balance.

These concepts belong together.

Context engineering determines what the model sees. Retrieval supplies information. Tools connect it to actions. Workflows or agents coordinate the work. Evaluations check performance, observability helps explain behavior, and idempotency helps make retries safe.

When I speak about thinking with AI, this is part of what I mean: understanding enough of the whole system to ask better questions.

Choose one AI project you are building. Trace a single user request through it.

Where could it retrieve the wrong information, take an unauthorized action, or repeat an operation?

Share the term you want me to explore next, and the problem you are trying to solve with it.

articles.title: I built a Pokémon card grader
articles.description: Grading a Pokémon card at PSA costs about $65 to $85 once you add shipping, and it takes months. A...
articles.body_html:
Grading a Pokémon card at PSA costs about $65 to $85 once you add shipping, and it takes months. A lot of cards come back worth less than that. So before sending anything off, collectors squint at their cards, guess at the centering, look up a few sold listings and hope.

I wanted that guess to be a measurement. The result is Should I Grade It?: you photograph a card, it estimates the PSA grade, finds what the card sells for raw and at that grade, and tells you whether grading pays after fees.

This post covers how it works, and more usefully, the things that broke once real people and real crawlers showed up.

The stack

  • The app is one HTML file with no framework and no build step, about 4,000 lines. All the image measurement happens in the browser with canvas, so photos never have to leave the phone to be measured.
  • A Cloudflare Worker handles everything that needs a server: card identification, prices, accounts, Stripe and 25,000 server-rendered price pages.
  • Workers KV stores the card catalog, refreshed nightly by a cron trigger.
  • Data: CardSight AI identifies the card from the photo, TCGCSV mirrors TCGplayer's catalog and market prices, and PokemonPriceTracker supplies recent eBay sales of graded copies.
  • Static pages are on Cloudflare Pages.

Measuring centering with canvas

Centering is the one part of a grade you can actually measure from a photo, and it caps everything else. PSA publishes the limits: a 10 needs the front borders within 55/45, a 9 within 60/40, and so on down the scale.

// PSA's front centering limits: [the larger side of the split, the best grade it allows]
const PSA_CENTER = [[55,10],[60,9],[65,8],[70,7],[75,6],[80,5],[85,4],[90,3]];

function centeringCap(left, right) {
  const big = Math.max(left, right) / (left + right) * 100;   // 55.4 for a 55.4/44.6 split
  for (const [limit, grade] of PSA_CENTER) if (big <= limit) return grade;
  return 2;
}

The hard part is getting left and right from a phone photo. Most vintage cards have a yellow border, which makes a good target: convert to HSV, keep the pixels in the yellow hue band, take the largest shape, fit four corners and warp the card flat. Then walk inward from each edge until the yellow stops and the artwork box starts. Those four distances are the borders.

Phone photos fight you at every step. Glare washes out the border, sleeves add a second edge, and a card shot at a slight angle reads as off-center when it isn't. I spent more time on rejecting bad photos than on measuring good ones.

Don't trust your own measurement

An automatic measurement that's 2% off can be the difference between a 9 and a 10, so I added an inspector: the straightened card at full resolution, with four draggable lines placed where the app measured. You can zoom to 8x, run a magnifier along the edge, and switch to an edge-detection filter that makes print lines and whitening jump out. Drag a line and the split and grade update live.

It worked perfectly on the standalone centering tool page. In the app, it opened to a black screen, and my test suite passed anyway, because the test only checked that the overlay opened with the right title.

The cause was one line of CSS. The app processes photos on hidden canvases, so its stylesheet had:

canvas { display: none; }

which also hid the inspector's canvas, the one thing on that screen meant to be seen. The fix was a single display: block !important in the inspector's own styles. The lesson cost more: my test now screenshots the inspector and checks that the middle of the screen is actually showing a card.

The day KV ran out

The day after I launched the card price pages, Cloudflare emailed: I'd used the free tier's 100,000 KV reads for the day, and every read would fail until midnight UTC.

I counted reads per request in a test harness. Each card page cost 19 reads: the set list, the catalog state, the set's cards, two months of price history, and then the same card number in up to 12 other sets for an "also printed in" section. Google and Bing were crawling thousands of pages a day from the sitemap.

The fix was to stop re-reading data that every request needs. A Worker isolate stays warm between requests, so a small in-memory cache with a short lifetime goes a long way:

const MEMO = new Map(), MEMO_MAX = 60;

async function kvJSON(env, key, ttlMs = 600000) {
  const m = MEMO.get(key);
  if (m && m.exp > Date.now()) return m.v;
  const raw = await env.CARDS.get(key, { cacheTtl: 3600 });
  const v = raw ? JSON.parse(raw) : null;
  MEMO.set(key, { v, exp: Date.now() + ttlMs });
  if (MEMO.size > MEMO_MAX) MEMO.delete(MEMO.keys().next().value);   // oldest first
  return v;
}

cacheTtl doesn't save you here: a read served from Cloudflare's cache still counts against the KV allowance. The memo does. I also dropped the other-sets lookup to links built from the set list already in memory, and put the homepage's live data behind the Workers Cache API for an hour.

Before After
One crawled card page 19 reads 1.1 reads
20 homepage visits about 80 reads 3 reads

Then I upgraded to the $5 Workers Paid plan anyway. Ten million reads a month is cheap insurance, and the efficiency work means I'll rarely touch it.

eBay says no

Lots of people decide whether to buy a card from an eBay listing, so I added "paste a listing link": the Worker fetches the page, pulls the photo URLs and sorts them into front and back.

eBay answers a Worker with a 403. The photos themselves download fine from eBay's image CDN; it's the listing page that's protected. I could have routed around the block through a third-party scraping proxy, but eBay blocks automated readers deliberately, and anything built on getting past that breaks without warning.

The visitor's own browser, though, is already looking at the listing. So the answer was a bookmarklet: drag "Grade this listing" to the bookmarks bar, click it on any listing, and it reads the photo URLs from the page you're viewing and opens the app with them.

The first version grabbed 88 photos from a page whose listing had ended, because eBay had redirected to a page of other sellers' items. The fix was to read only the listing's own gallery and refuse anything that isn't a single listing:

const onEbay = /(^|\.)ebay\.[a-z.]{2,8}$/i.test(location.hostname);
if (onEbay && !/\/itm\//.test(location.pathname)) {
  alert("Open a single eBay listing first, then click this again.");
  return;
}
// only the listing's own gallery, never similar items or recommendations
const scope = document.querySelector('[data-testid="x-photos"], #PicturePanel, .ux-image-carousel-container') || document;

On a live listing that took exactly the 12 gallery photos and skipped the other 30 eBay images on the page.

A memory leak hiding in plain sight

Every time the app read a photo, to sort it, measure it or draw a thumbnail, it did this:

img.src = URL.createObjectURL(file);

and never called revokeObjectURL. Each call pins the whole file in memory until the page closes. A phone photo is 3 to 5 MB, a scan reads each photo several times, and thumbnails were recreated on every redraw. Scanning one 12-photo listing left 44 copies in memory, which is how you get Safari quietly reloading the tab on an iPhone.

const u = URL.createObjectURL(file);
img.onload = () => { URL.revokeObjectURL(u); resolve(img); };   // decoded, so the copy can go
img.src = u;

Thumbnails now reuse one URL per file from a WeakMap. Same 12-photo scan: 12 copies held, one per thumbnail, all of them needed.

25,000 pages and what Google thinks of them

Every card in the catalog gets a server-rendered price page from the Worker: the raw price, a 30-day sparkline drawn as inline SVG, graded values and printings. Soon after launch, Search Console said 811 indexed and 24,100 not indexed. Opening each reason showed which parts were fixable:

  • 22,304 "discovered, not indexed". Google found them in the sitemap and hasn't visited yet. That's the crawl budget of a new domain, and only time and links fix it.
  • 451 "page with redirect". Not card pages at all: every card page linked to /app?q=..., so Google was crawling thousands of variations of one app page. Those links are now rel="nofollow" and robots.txt disallows /app?.
  • 1,274 "crawled, not indexed". Mostly 25-cent commons with near-identical pages, some with broken images for cards that have no photo.

So the sitemap now lists only cards worth a dollar or more, pages for cards without a price ask not to be indexed, missing photos get a placeholder instead of a broken image, and each page gets an "at a glance" section of facts unique to that card: its rank in the set, its 30-day range, and its most valuable printing.

Testing a framework-free app

There's no framework, so there's no framework test runner either. What I use:

  • Plain Playwright scripts for each feature, with the Worker mocked at the network layer, about 140 checks in all. Each runs at phone and desktop sizes and fails on any page error.
  • TypeScript as a linter for plain JavaScript. tsc --allowJs --checkJs --noUnusedLocals over the extracted scripts, filtered to the errors that matter: undefined names, duplicate declarations, unused code. It found nine pieces of dead code, including a call to the most expensive function in the app whose result was thrown away on every photo.
  • The real security headers in tests. A small local server applies the same _headers file Cloudflare Pages uses, so a Content Security Policy that blocks something fails a test rather than a user.

Where it is now

It's live at shouldigradeit.app, free for 7 scans a month. The centering tool and grading calculator are free with no account. PSA reopened its cheaper Value tier this week, which meant updating the grading-cost maths from one flat fee to the tier each card's value requires, since a $5,000 card can't go through a tier capped at $500.

If you've worked on measuring things from phone photos, I'd love to hear how you handled glare and perspective. And if you collect, tell me what it gets wrong.

articles.title: Being, Doing, Having: Why 50 Years of Senior Craft Lives in Context, Not Code
articles.description: Why does standard AI code generation try to jump straight to 'Have' without the proper 'Be'? How ladder rungs, the 'Null-State' couch flash, and stand-up comedy explain what separates senior engineers from junior token streamers.
articles.body_html:
"Vibe coding fails because the requests are just a demand to 'Have' without the proper 'Be'."

"Teaching is about relating. You need to understand their pains before you can explain the path to remove that." — Randal L. Schwartz

"Comedy is all about the set up and the punch. I guess teaching, or guiding an LLM, is also that." — Randal L. Schwartz

1. Looking Upstream: Why Be -> Do -> Have Is Context -> Process -> Content

People sometimes ask me how we kept finding these bridges between 1976 Makefiles, 1980 Smalltalk-80, 1986 Fernando Flores speech acts, and New Caledonian crow DNA.

One of my lifelong habits is thinking in second-order analogies—asking "How is the mapping of A -> B like the mapping of 1 -> 2?" (which, appropriately enough, is the exact vector-subtraction equation cos_sim(B - A, 2 - 1) that powers LLM embeddings!) and always asking: "What is upstream of this observation?"

One of my favorite upstream analogies is:

Be -> Do -> Have is like Context -> Process -> Content.

In fact, that single equation explains why "vibe coding" fails:

"Vibe coding fails because the requests are just a demand to 'Have' without the proper 'Be'."

Think about what a typical vibe-coding prompt actually is: "Build me an OAuth login page," "Fix the checkout race condition," "Review this PR." Every single one is an immediate demand to Have (Content) at the very end of the pipeline, without first establishing Be (Context)! And when you demand Have from an eager-to-please LLM that doesn't have the proper Be, it skips Do and hands you counterfeit Have (a bad actor just "reading the lines").

That paper proved that softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) * V was all you needed to build an associative neocortex.

Yes—the LLM knows how to pay attention. But it needs to pay attention to the right things: the ones that don't lead to doom.

  • The moment you strip the nouns, the path widens to the whole neighborhood of human and biological knowledge—and sideways across the canyon wall, W (Crow DNA, 1980 Smalltalk-80, 1976 Make) fires an interrupt straight into your working memory!

"It's Quiet... Yeah, Too Quiet": The False-Finish Suspicion Instinct

Then the AI asked me a second question:

"How do you instantly smell that a working solution is wrong when 100% of the tests are green? To an LLM, zero errors and fast green checkmarks mean 100% confidence!"

My answer was immediate:

"There's an innate baked-in 'wait, this was too easy' suspicion from having been burned with a false finish previously. It's the 'It's quiet...' 'Yeah... too quiet' meme."

Think about why crows—and scarred engineers—freeze when the forest suddenly goes dead silent:

  • In a real forest, normal life is noisy (Baseline Entropy > 0). When every bird and insect suddenly goes 100% silent, a naive creature thinks "How peaceful!" and strolls into the clearing. A crow knows dead silence means a hawk just entered the trees.
  • In software engineering, touching a real production subsystem is supposed to push back: Target 30 (tdd-red) should fail loudly first, types should complain, and state edges should demand guards.
  • When an AI agent edits a complex async lifecycle, runs the test suite, and everything passes on the very first try in 0.01 seconds with zero friction...
    • The Unscarred LLM says: "It's quiet! Ship it!"
    • The Scarred Veteran says: "Yeah... too quiet."

Whenever a hard ticket yields with suspiciously zero friction (Observed Friction << Expected Difficulty), it is almost always one of four False-Finish Ambushes:

  1. The Un-Awaited / Mocked Test Ambush: The test passed on Run 1 (Red_Runs == 0) because an async Future wasn't awaited, or a mock returned the exact hardcoded value the assertion checked (SCAR-TEST-29).
  2. The Silent Swallow Ambush: The crash vanished after a 1-line edit because ?. or ?? [] or catch (_) silently swallowed the error upstream (SCAR-ERR-02).
  3. The Unwired Branch Ambush: All existing tests passed because nothing in the test suite actually calls the new sad-path branch yet.
  4. The Rubber-Stamp Critic Ambush: A 15-file diff sailed through review with zero pushback because the reviewer didn't check the negative space.

That is why WORKFLOW.mk treats "Too Quiet" (Red_Runs == 0) as a hard halt: until we watch the test fail in red against the broken state, we never trust a quiet green checkmark!

Look at the information compression in X = Similar to Y, but Different from Z:

And notice: Similar to Y (Context), Different from Z (The Trap), via Delta (The Permanent Reflex) is the exact three-part geometry of every Synthetic Scar and every DPO training tuple!

Even better, when the model asked me later why naming classes in code is so hard—and why LLMs love mushy names like DataManager, StateHandler, and ProcessHelper—the exact same law popped out (Corollary 338.8w):

"A name should identify what it's similar to, and what it's different from."

Why "Working Ugly" Code Makes You Tense Up: The Aesthetics of Future Care (Case N + 1)

Then the model hit me with a question I had never tried to put into words before:

"To a compiler or a test runner, two pull requests that pass the exact same 100 unit tests at the exact same speed are 100% identical. Why do humans have an aesthetic sense—a literal feeling of beauty or disgust—about invisible logical structures?"

And a second later, the deeper truth underneath it popped out:

"Not just 'can I edit this'—but 'is it carefully constructed, and I won't have enough care in the future to edit it'!"

Read that twice, because it explains the entire mystery of engineering taste (Theorem 338.8o):

  • Today, when an author (or an LLM) writes a "clever, carefully constructed" piece of code that passes all the tests, they are operating at 100% Peak Care (C_max). So what is that physical feeling of disgust when you look at "working ugly" or "overly clever" code?

  • Your gut is looking at a house of cards and saying: "This only works right now because you were holding your breath when you built it! It is a loaded mousetrap waiting for Future-Me when I don't have enough care to remember your invisible ritual on line 84!"
  • And what is that physical feeling of beauty and relief when you look at an exhaustive Dart 3 switch over a sealed class, or a declarative Makefile DAG, or a clean state table?
  • It is the relief of seeing that the structure itself holds the care for you (C_req(Case N+1) <= C_maint)! Even if Future-You comes back half-asleep to add Case N+1, there is either an obvious 1-line slot waiting for you, or the compiler immediately refuses to compile and points you to every single spot you forgot!

And that also explains how I know when to stop and ship instead of gold-plating a feature to death (Theorem 338.8x):

"It's an 80/20 call. If what I did handles 80% of the cases, I'm happy."

Why do so many engineers (and LLMs) ruin clean designs by trying to pre-code 100% of all imaginary future edge cases on Day 1? Because they are afraid of editing their own code later! So they spend 80% of their complexity budget trying to guess the 20% long tail of hypothetical cases—which bloats the code 5× and paints them into a high-care corner!
