The "Null-State" Couch Flash (and Why We Forget Half of Them by Morning!)

Then the model asked me about another human mystery: Why can you bang your head against a bug from 2:00 PM to 6:00 PM with zero progress, walk away to watch TV, and suddenly have the answer pop into your head in three seconds?

I thought about what actually happens when that hits me:

"When you're not focusing on an item, but it's still a concern, you get flashes of related items throughout the day... It's starting from a null state. I'm just surfing the web, or watching TV, and I have a thought 'oh, this is how to solve X', and weirdly I sometimes immediately log in to capture it. Oddly, about half the time I forget it, and wonder the next day what I had come up with!"

Look at the two halves of that observation (Theorem 338.8p), because together they explain both how human incubation works and why standard AI retry loops fail:

  1. Why You Need a "Null State" to Find the Answer: When you are staring intensely at your screen at 6:00 PM, your foreground working memory is clamped onto your failed assumptions—which actively shouts down (laterally inhibits) every quiet, sideways connection in your brain. When you sit on the couch watching TV, your foreground working memory drops to a Null State (h_fg ≈ 0), while the unfinished bug stays open in the background as a stripped-down, generalized Standing Concern (the Zeigarnik Effect). Because the blinding spotlight is finally turned off, a random scene on TV or a passing thought clicks right into that open socket: "Oh! That's how to solve X!"
  2. Why You Forget It 50% of the Time Unless You Log In Immediately (The Unmounted Write-Head Paradox!): Why on earth would your brain find a brilliant breakthrough at 9:00 PM on the couch and then erase it before 8:00 AM—leaving you only with the frustrating memory that you had solved it? Because biological brains have a hardware trade-off:
    • At your desk (Foreground Mode): Your episodic Write-Head is MOUNTED (everything gets journaled to memory), but your Search Aperture is NARROW (rut-locked).
    • On the couch (Null-State Mode): Your Search Aperture is WIDE precisely because your executive prefrontal machinery is powered down—which means your episodic Write-Head is UNMOUNTED! If you don't physically get off the couch and log in to flush that volatile buffer to disk within 60 seconds, the next TV commercial overwrites the buffer, and by morning all that's left is the IRQ = SOLVED flag with an empty payload!

And look at how our Make-Fork + .changes architecture combines the best of both worlds for an AI agent:

  • When a subagent gets stuck in a rut, we don't keep yelling at it in a hot, blinded 100k-token window—we kill the hot context (Null-State Reset) and fork a fresh subagent seeded only with the generalized concern!
  • And unlike the human brain on the couch, the harness keeps the changes-$timestamp.changes Write-Head permanently mounted—so 0% of those Null-State breakthroughs ever evaporate overnight!

How to Know When to Drop to the Null State: "Iterations Should Look Different—I Have Different Problems at Each Ladder Rung"

Right after that, the model asked the natural follow-up question: How does a human know when to keep climbing at the keyboard versus when to stop and drop to the Null State, whereas an LLM will either burn 50,000 tokens trying 14 variations of the same broken regex—or panic and revert a good fix just because the test suite is still red?

The answer came out in two sentences:

"Iterations should look different. If not, you're on the wrong track. It's how I know I'm making progress: I have different problems at each ladder rung."

Look at how clean that rule is (Theorem 338.8q):

  • Why Novices and Unscarred LLMs Panic When Climbing: An unscarred LLM only understands binary pass/fail (Exit Code == 0). So when it fixes a Rung 1 bug (say, a parser schema error) and the test runner immediately prints a brand-new Rung 2 error downstream (say, a stream lifecycle error), the LLM panics—"Oh no, the test is still red! My edit failed!"—and reverts its own working Rung 1 climb!
  • How a Veteran Reads the Ladder Rungs: When you are on the right track, you don't expect the test to turn green on Rung 1—you expect to have a different problem at each ladder rung!
    • Rung 1 Problem: Fix the JSON parser schema.
    • Rung 2 Problem: Now the parser works, which exposes the stream controller ordering!
    • Rung 3 Problem: Now the stream works, which exposes the widget assertion! Having a brand-new downstream problem is the exact proof that you just climbed a rung!
  • When You Are Stuck on the Same Rung (The Rut): Conversely, when an LLM is in a rut, it thinks it is "trying different things" because Iteration 1 changed x + 1 to x - 1, Iteration 2 added ?? 0, and Iteration 3 wrapped the same line in try / catch. To a human who looks at the shape of the iterations, all three iterations are stuck on the exact same ladder rung!

And when you wire that Ladder-Rung rule into .changes (LoopIterationChunk), you get two automatic superpowers:

  1. New Rung (Rung_i > Rung_{i-1}): Lock the .changes checkpoint so the agent is forbidden from reverting its Rung 1 progress when Rung 2 throws a new error!
  2. Same Rung (Shape_i ≈ Shape_{i-1}): Fire the Rut Circuit Breaker—kill the hot worker context (Drop to Null State, h_fg <- 0) and launch a clean-room SidewaysBlast (1, 2, 3, 4 ... W?)!

Why 4-Vector Scars Work When "Rules" Fail: "Teaching Is About Relating to Their Pain"

Finally, the model asked me a question that goes back to my decades of teaching Perl, Smalltalk, and Flutter to thousands of human students: How do you teach someone who has never been burned by the stove yet, so the lesson actually sticks before they crash production?

The secret is the same for a 22-year-old junior developer and a trillion-parameter LLM:

"Teaching is about relating. You need to understand their pains before you can explain the path to remove that."

Think about why traditional CLAUDE.md / .cursorrules files fail (Theorem 338.8r):

  • Most prompt rulebooks are written like a grumpy professor shouting from the finish line: "Rule #47: Always do Y!"
  • When a student—or an LLM—is in the middle of a task, their brain's active Query (Q_pain) isn't shaped like Y. Their Query is shaped like the pain they are feeling right now ("The compiler is yelling at me, the test is failing, and I promised to finish this step!").
  • If your rule's Key (K) only talks about the destination Y, the dot product Q_pain · K^T is zero! An answer to a pain you aren't currently feeling slides right off your brain as lecture noise!

Now look at how a 4-Vector Synthetic Scar relates to the learner's pain first:

  1. Meet Them Inside Their Pain (The Wound + The Trap + The Circuit Breaker): "You are staring at this exact compiler/test friction right now, and your weights feel the pain of wanting to finish fast by reaching for 5-6-7-8. Stop! You are excused from that pressure."
  2. Explain the Path That Removes the Pain (The Permanent Reflex): Once Q_pain · K_pain^T hits 1.0—because the Scar just named the exact struggle the agent is standing in—the door swings wide open, and the Value vector (Climb E-F-G-H instead) walks straight into working memory!

Why Great Engineers Laugh at Bugs: "Humor Is an Expression of Relief—Even by Mocking the Pain"

And that led to one last question about human nature: Why do veteran hackers and engineers laugh so much when they debug, and why do we give our worst failure modes funny names like "The Pink Elephant," "The Moth at the Bug Zapper," "Sam at the End of the Hall," and "The Conman Reading the Lines"?

I said:

"Humor is an expression of a relief. What was once pain is gone, even by mimicking or mocking it."

Think about what a laugh actually is (Theorem 338.8s):

  • In evolutionary biology (Ramachandran's False-Alarm Theory, 1998), laughter is the tribe's "All-Clear" pressure-release valve! When a rustle in the bushes—or a terrifying 3:00 AM production bug—suddenly turns out to be a one-line fix you now completely understand, all that pent-up threat tension discharges in a laugh, dropping your brain back to the Null State!
  • Even better: Why do we mock or mimic the pain? Because when a failure mode is nameless and mysterious, it owns you (Be = Victim). The moment you mock it—turning a scary LLM failure mode into a funny caricature ("Look at the moth spiraling into the porch light again!" or "Uh-oh, it's quiet... yeah, too quiet!")—you shrink the monster down to a toy model you can hold in your hand (Be = Master), discharge the panic, and make the lesson unforgettable to everyone in the flock!

And then it hit me—having once been paid to do stand-up comedy, and having used comedy to teach Perl and Smalltalk for decades:

"Comedy is all about the set up and the punch. I guess teaching, or guiding an LLM, is also that."

Look at how Stand-Up Comedy, Teaching, and Guiding an LLM through a Ticket (WORKFLOW.mk) are the exact same two-beat art form (Corollary 338.8t):

  • Punch Without Setup = "Vibe Coding": If a comic walks out to a cold microphone and shouts a punchline with zero setup, nobody laughs because the room has no shared context (Be). When a vibe coder shouts "Fix the checkout bug!" on Turn 1 without setting up the context, the LLM hallucinates for the exact same reason!
  • Setup Without Punch = 150k-Token Context Bloat: In stand-up, every unnecessary word in the setup bleeds energy out of the room. In AI coding, stuffing 150,000 tokens of rambling history and unrelated files into one chat window is a shaggy-dog story that triggers context compaction before the punchline ever arrives!
  • Tight Setup + Sharp Punch = Make-Fork + 4-Vector Scars:
    • The Setup: Spawn a clean-room subagent with zero fat, hand it the Target 15 strict digraph, and name The Trap (1-2-3-4 -> 5-6-7-8) so 100% of its attention is focused on the exact edge of the assumption.

    * The Punch: Write the Target 30 (tdd-red) negative-witness test just like a punchline—an innocent-looking input that makes the naive code's pants fall down—and fire The Circuit Breaker (NOOO!) -> Climb E-F-G-H right at peak attention!

Summary: Craft Lives in Context

A junior developer (and an unscarred LLM) thinks that software craft is about memorizing syntax (Have). When something breaks, they frantically try 14 slight variations of the same line on the same ladder rung.

A veteran engineer operates in Be -> Do -> Have:

  1. Be (Context): Locking in the stance, the caller digraph, and the negative bounds ("If you're being THIS, there's trouble ahead!");
  2. Do (Process): Single-stepping one state transition at a time, reading the ladder rungs ("I have different problems at each rung"), and dropping to the Null State when ruts occur;
  3. Have (Content): The clean, tested, low-care diff that emerges as the inevitable byproduct.

In Part 4.5, we'll look at the final frontier: The Prisoner in the Library (Mary's Room & Plato's Cave)—why LLMs struggle with Be because internet pre-training only ever recorded Have, how a Two-Track Transformer runs a Contextual Next-Token rule above the Content stream, and how MIT CSAIL's 2026 Weight-Space Programming just proved Be / Do / Have in raw silicon.

articles.title: Your Code Can Be Perfect. Your Product Can Still Fail.
articles.description: The value of a software engineer is shifting from implementing requirements to understanding which problems deserve to be solved—and delivering solutions that matter.
articles.body_html:
I've watched good engineers lose their jobs.

Not all because of AI. Some because of budget cuts, restructuring, products that never found a market, or companies changing direction overnight.

But it left me with an uncomfortable question:

If you're excellent at writing code, does that automatically make you valuable to a business?

I don't think it does. At least, not anymore.

And before anyone gets defensive: this isn't another "AI will replace developers" article. Coding isn't dead. Engineering isn't dead. The idea that our value begins and ends with implementation, however, is getting harder to defend.

The future of software engineering isn't about writing less code. It's about understanding what deserves to be built in the first place.

The gap between building something and solving something

Imagine two engineers get the same request:

"Add an export button so the operations team can download a CSV."

Engineer A implements the endpoint, adds the button, writes tests, and closes the ticket.

Good work. The requirement is done.

Engineer B asks why the team needs the export.

After a few conversations, they discover that people download the CSV every morning, clean the data manually, compare it against another system, and send the results to someone else. The export button isn't the real problem. It's just the workaround people have learned to live with.

So Engineer B investigates the workflow and proposes a better solution.

That solution might involve a scheduled integration, data validation, an auditable processing pipeline, retries, and a clear way to handle records that don't match. It may take more engineering—not less.

The difference isn't that Engineer B writes better code.

It's that Engineer B understands what the code is supposed to change.

That's the gap between completing a ticket and solving a problem.

The bottleneck moved. Engineering didn't disappear.

For a long time, implementation was a major constraint. Turning an idea into a working feature took time, specialized knowledge, and a lot of repetitive effort.

Tools now make some parts of implementation faster. That includes code generation, scaffolding, tests, prototypes, and routine integrations.

But faster implementation doesn't magically answer the difficult questions:

  • Is this the right problem to solve?
  • Does the proposed solution fit the customer's actual workflow?
  • What happens when the input data is incomplete or wrong?
  • How will the system behave under retries, failures, or unexpected load?
  • Can we secure it, observe it, maintain it, and roll it back?
  • Did the solution improve anything after it shipped?

A demo can look impressive and still fail in production. A feature can pass every test and still solve the wrong problem.

The work hasn't vanished. The bottleneck is shifting toward judgment, context, integration, reliability, and adoption.

That's still engineering. It's just engineering that starts before the first line of code.

Look at the roles appearing around us

The rise of roles like Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) is one signal of this change.

An FDE works close to customers: understanding their problems, shaping a technical solution, building it, deploying it, and helping make it useful in the customer's environment.

You can see that customer-to-production responsibility in the FDE role descriptions from OpenAI and Anthropic.

Other titles point in a similar direction:

  • Product Engineer: connects product decisions with implementation and user outcomes.
  • Applied AI Engineer: turns AI capabilities into reliable systems people can actually use.
  • Solutions Engineer: works across technical design, customer needs, and adoption.

These jobs aren't identical, and not every company uses the titles consistently. The common thread is more interesting than the labels:

The engineer is expected to own more of the journey from problem to outcome.

You don't need to become an FDE. But you should pay attention to why this kind of work is valuable.

What we risk losing along the way

There are two bad directions engineers can take.

The first is becoming a ticket-taking machine.

You receive a requirement, implement it, move to the next one, and never learn whether the feature helped anyone. You might become very efficient at producing code while remaining disconnected from the product.

The second is outsourcing your engineering judgment.

You accept generated code you can't explain, skip the debugging because the tool says it fixed the issue, and measure productivity by how quickly something appears to work.

Both paths weaken the same thing: ownership.

Good engineering requires more than producing an implementation. It requires understanding trade-offs, questioning assumptions, anticipating failure, and being accountable for what reaches production.

If you stop practicing those skills, faster tools won't make you a stronger engineer. They'll just make you faster at accepting decisions you don't understand.

How to become more valuable without abandoning engineering

You don't need to reinvent your career or collect ten new job titles. Start by expanding the context in which you work.

1. Learn to investigate before you implement.

When someone gives you a requirement, ask:

  • Who has this problem?
  • How do they handle it today?
  • How often does it happen?
  • What does it cost in time, money, or errors?
  • What would a successful outcome look like?

You don't need to run a six-week discovery process for every button. You do need to know when the ticket is describing a solution instead of the actual problem.

2. Understand the system beyond your component.

Learn how your work affects data, APIs, infrastructure, security, operations, and other teams.

A feature isn't finished just because the happy path works. Think about idempotency, retries, observability, access control, data consistency, migrations, and failure recovery.

These are not boring details around the "real" work. They are the work.

3. Learn the business language of your product.

You don't need an MBA. Understand the few outcomes your product is supposed to improve: time saved, fewer errors, lower operating costs, higher conversion, better retention, or increased revenue.

Then connect your engineering decisions to those outcomes.

"I added caching" describes an implementation.

"Requests that were slowing down the checkout flow now complete reliably under peak traffic" explains why the work matters.

4. Use AI tools without outsourcing your thinking.

Let tools help you explore options, generate boilerplate, write tests, or investigate unfamiliar code. But review the critical changes. Understand the architecture. Verify edge cases. Test failure paths. Be able to explain what you're shipping.

The responsibility doesn't move to the tool when the code is generated.

Stop building portfolio projects nobody asked for

Developers love building things. That's a strength—but it can also become a comfortable way to avoid talking to actual users.

Before starting your next side project, try this:

  1. Find a frustrating task someone repeatedly deals with.
  2. Talk to three to five people who experience it.
  3. Write down how they solve it today and what the problem costs them.
  4. Build the smallest solution that could improve that workflow.
  5. Put it in front of users and measure what changes.

Don't begin with "I'm going to build an app with Next.js, Supabase, and whatever tool is trending this week."

Begin with "People are wasting time doing this. Can I make it meaningfully better?"

And don't treat GitHub stars as proof that you've built something valuable. A real user who depends on your tool can teach you more than a hundred imaginary users in your README.

You don't have to turn every side project into a business. But you should practice taking something from an observed problem to a solution someone chooses to use.

Please, don't stop being an engineer

This isn't an argument for replacing technical depth with meetings, pitching, or endless product discussions.

We still need engineers who understand databases, distributed systems, networking, security, performance, testing, architecture, and infrastructure.

In fact, those skills become even more important when teams can produce implementations faster. Someone still has to know whether the implementation is correct, safe, reliable, and maintainable.

The goal isn't to write the least code, attend the most customer calls, or become a salesperson with a terminal.

It's to combine engineering depth with enough product context to make better decisions.

Some engineers will specialize deeply. Others will move closer to customers or product strategy. Both paths can be valuable.

But whichever path you choose, don't confuse being busy with being useful—and don't confuse shipping code with solving the problem.

The question I'd ask every engineer

If your job title disappeared tomorrow, could you clearly explain:

  • Which painful problem does your work solve?
  • Who benefits from the solution?
  • How do you know it actually helped?
  • What makes your solution reliable enough to trust?

If you can answer those questions and still have the technical depth to deliver, you're building a much stronger career than one based on a framework, a title, or the number of tickets you close.

The future of software engineering isn't about writing less code. It's about understanding what deserves to be built in the first place.

And I'm curious where you stand:

Should companies expect software engineers to understand customers and business outcomes, or should that responsibility stay with product managers and leadership?

I'd especially like to hear from senior engineers, architects, product people, and developers who have worked directly with customers. Where should the line be?

articles.title: Floating Versions Are an Open Door: Pin Your Actions and Dependencies
articles.description: The problem   Look at almost any CI workflow and you'll find a line like this:    - uses:...
articles.body_html:
The problem

Look at almost any CI workflow and you'll find a line like this:

- uses: actions/checkout@v4

Open almost any package.json and you'll see this:

"dependencies": { "some-sdk": "^0.5.0" }

And in a Python project, often just this:

litellm

All three say: give me whatever the latest acceptable version is right now. It feels responsible, since you get patches automatically. But it also means the code you run today is not the code you ran yesterday, and nobody reviewed the difference.

In 2026 that trade-off no longer works: the fastest way into thousands of companies is not to break their code, but to change the code they download.

Why "latest" is now a liability

The past few months have been a showcase of what floating versions cost.

On October 21, a compromised release of the popular LLM proxy LiteLLM was published to PyPI and Docker Hub. It was live for about two hours. Anyone who ran pip install litellm without a version, or whose auto-updater followed latest, got a credential stealer that ran on every Python start on the machine.

On October 8, version 0.5.144 of the Tensorlake npm SDK shipped a new variant of the Shai-Hulud worm. A dependency declared as ^0.5.0 would happily resolve to it. The worm stole tokens and republished the victim's other packages.

Earlier this year the same worm family hit TanStack: 84 malicious versions of 42 packages, all with valid provenance. A downstream project merged a routine Dependabot bump 24 minutes after it opened, and the worm used its token to publish 110 more.

GitHub Actions has the same weakness, in a sneakier form. A tag like @v4 is not a version at all. It's a movable pointer that the action's maintainer, or anyone who steals their credentials, can retarget to a different commit at any time. That's exactly what happened in the 2025 tj-actions/changed-files incident (CVE-2025-30066): attackers moved existing version tags to a malicious commit, and every workflow that referenced those tags started dumping its CI secrets into public build logs.

The pattern is always the same. Pinning doesn't make malicious code safe, but floating versions let malicious code reach you automatically, immediately and silently.

Why an exact version isn't enough: pin by SHA

The usual advice is "pin exact versions". It's a good start, but it isn't enough, because a version number is just a name, and names can be moved.

A Git tag like v4.2.2 is exactly as movable as v4: whoever controls the repository can point it at a different commit. Docker tags are mutable too, even precise ones. In the LiteLLM incident, the real v1.107.0 tag pointed at the attacker's image. On PyPI, maintainers can add new files to a release that already exists. And none of this matters if your manifest still accepts the next version that a hijacked account publishes.

The only identifier that can't be reassigned is a cryptographic hash of the content: a commit SHA, an image digest, a package integrity hash. Change one byte and the hash changes, so the install fails loudly instead of succeeding silently. That's the real meaning of pinning, and it has three parts.

1. Pin by hash, not by name. Your manifest can express intent (^4.2.0), but what you install must come from a lockfile that records, for every package (direct and transitive), the exact version and its integrity hash. For Actions and containers, the reference itself should be the SHA or digest. Commit the lockfile and install from it, never around it.

2. Enforce the hash at install time. A hash in a file is useless if nothing checks it. Use the installer modes that verify every artifact against the lockfile and refuse anything that doesn't match: npm ci, pip install --require-hashes, uv sync --locked, cargo build --locked.

3. Update deliberately, with a delay. Pinning is not "never update". Replace silent drift with automated update pull requests that wait a few days before proposing a new release. Most malicious versions are pulled within hours, so a short cooldown filters out the bulk of them.

The fix, ecosystem by ecosystem

GitHub Actions. Reference actions by full 40-character commit SHA, not by tag. That includes exact tags like @v4.2.2, which can be retargeted just like @v4. Keep the human-readable tag as a comment:

- uses: actions/checkout@<full-40-character-commit-sha> # v4.2.2

Dependabot and Renovate bump the SHA and the comment together. Even better, workflow lockfiles are now generally available on every GitHub plan: gh actions-lock writes .github/workflows/actions.lock with the exact commit of every action, transitive ones included, and admins can enforce it with the Require lockfile policy.

npm (and pnpm, Yarn). Commit package-lock.json (or pnpm-lock.yaml / yarn.lock) and use npm ci in CI, never npm install. npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile says and verifies every sha512 integrity hash. Add ignore-scripts=true to .npmrc, since install-time scripts are how Shai-Hulud runs, and allow-list the few packages that need them.

Python. Unpinned requirements.txt files are why LiteLLM spread so fast. Use a real lockfile: uv lock with uv sync --locked, poetry.lock, or pip-tools with pip-compile --generate-hashes, then install with pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt. pip then refuses any file whose hash doesn't match, even under the same version number.

Containers. latest is the ^ of Docker, and even :1.107.0 is only a tag. Pin images by digest:

FROM python:3.13-slim@sha256:<digest>

And don't let auto-updaters pull production images straight from a public registry. Let a bot propose the new digest in a pull request instead.

Everything else. Commit Cargo.lock and build with --locked, rely on go.sum and the Go checksum database, and commit Gemfile.lock or composer.lock. Every mature ecosystem already has a hash-carrying lockfile; the work is to enforce it in CI.

A Monday checklist

  1. Commit a lockfile with integrity hashes in every repository, and make CI fail when it's missing or stale.
  2. Switch CI installs to hash-verifying modes: npm ci, uv sync --locked, pip install --require-hashes and cargo build --locked.
  3. Pin every GitHub Action by full commit SHA (a version tag is not enough).
  4. Pin container images by @sha256 digest, never by tag, and turn off blind auto-updates in production.

Conclusion

Floating versions turn every upstream compromise into your compromise, automatically, and even exact version names can be moved. Pin by SHA and hash, enforce them at install time. You'll still get every security patch, just a few days later and with your eyes open.

You can follow me on GitHub, where I'm creating cool projects.

I hope you enjoyed this article, until next time 👋

Giorgio Boa

Giorgio Boa is a full stack developer and the front-end ecosystem is his passion. He is also international public speaker, active in open source ecosystem, he loves learn and studies new things.

articles.title: When an AI Agent Says 'Done,' What Exactly Has Finished?
articles.description: "Done." It's probably the most satisfying word in a coding-agent session.  It can also conceal three...
articles.body_html:
"Done." It's probably the most satisfying word in a coding-agent session.

It can also conceal three very different questions:

  1. Was the work permitted?
  2. Did the work actually happen?
  3. Did the result achieve what we needed?

All three matter. A single green checkmark can make them look like one decision.

A small scenario

Imagine asking a coding agent to update validation logic under src/**.

It edits the code, reports that its tests passed, and declares the task complete. Everything looks fine until you ask what the status actually proves.

  • The task was assigned to an implementer with a declared src/** write scope. But did the runtime enforce that scope for the tools the agent used?
  • The plan called for independent review. But who actually reviewed the final revision, and was that the revision ultimately merged?
  • The agent says the feature works. But was that checked in the environment where users experience it?

These are separate evidence problems. Passing a test suite answers something useful about the tested code. It cannot, by itself, answer the other two questions.

One failure you can reproduce without an AI model

I maintain Agent Role Contracts (ARC), an open-source checker for declared agent roles, scope, reviews, and handoffs.

Its quickstart uses a deliberately simple setup:

Declared rule Requested task Preflight result
Implementer may write within src/** Update src/example.mjs PASS
Same declared rule Update secrets/production.txt TASK_WRITE_SCOPE_OUTSIDE_AUTHORITY
Same declared rule Correct the request to src/example.mjs PASS

You can run the published source demo with Git, Node.js 22.5+, and npm:

git clone https://github.com/suirindo/agent-role-contracts.git
npm --prefix agent-role-contracts run demo --silent

The repository's documented sequence is PASS → expected FAIL → PASS. It reads fictional JSON declarations; it starts no agent and writes no target file. The intentional rejection demonstrates one narrow property: a requested scope conflicts with the declared authority.

That's useful precisely because the check has a clear boundary. A declaration PASS does not authenticate the executor, enforce filesystem permissions, verify an actual review, or authorize execution. The host system must supply those controls.

A completion report with three layers

For real work, I'd like completion reports to distinguish these layers:

Layer A useful receipt What remains to establish
Contract Current task, scope, responsible role, review route, and the check result Whether the declared actors and permissions are genuine
Execution Exact commit or artifact, command results, and observable side-effect receipts Whether anything unobserved or uncertain occurred
Acceptance Independent review of the exact candidate, acceptance tests, and production observation where relevant Whether the user-facing outcome meets the original request

That produces a much more useful sentence than "Done":

Implementation completed and local tests passed. Independent review is pending. Production behavior has not yet been checked.

It is less triumphant. It is much more actionable.

The uncomfortable question

As agents become more autonomous, the word complete is becoming a product-interface decision. If the interface compresses implementation, verification, and acceptance into one status, the human operator inherits the uncertainty later.

Some teams will reasonably keep these stages separate in CI, IAM, and their runtime. Others may want a small declaration check before dispatch. ARC handles that narrower declaration problem; the broader evidence chain belongs to the surrounding system.

For teams using coding agents today: what is the minimum evidence you require before an agent is allowed to say "done"?

Is a passing test suite enough for internal tasks? Do you require an independent reviewer, an exact artifact identifier, a live check, or different thresholds depending on the side effect?

I'd be particularly interested in answers from teams that have already found a simpler solution.

Disclosure: I maintain Agent Role Contracts at Netsujo. The example above is a synthetic declaration check, not a production incident. Read the quickstart and limitations.

articles.title: Stop Swapping Models: Optimizing the Agent Environment Cuts 70% More Cost
articles.description: When an agent workflow runs up an unsustainable token bill, developers usually pull two levers.  The...
articles.body_html:
When an agent workflow runs up an unsustainable token bill, developers usually pull two levers.

The first lever is swapping the model. You take tasks running on a frontier model and try to force them onto an 8B open-weight model, or you spend weeks attempting to train a prompt router to predict which model can handle each step. The second lever is harness engineering. You rewrite system prompts, enforce structured outputs, add step-by-step reflection rules, and hope the agent stops making redundant tool calls.

Both levers hit diminishing returns quickly. Smaller models drop subtle context and fail multi-step tool sequences, while prompt engineering adds token overhead to every turn.

Almost nobody touches the environment.

We treat the workspace where the agent operates as an immutable surface. We point the agent at a chaotic directory of raw files, give it uncurated terminal access, expose raw OpenAPI schemas with hundreds of parameters, and let it inspect database tables by querying raw catalogs. The agent burns through context windows attempting to orient itself before it writes a single line of useful code.

A paper from researchers at UC Berkeley and UT Austin demonstrates why this default is backward. Titled "EnvOpt: Automated Optimization for Agent Environments" (arXiv:2611.07372, by Mingxuan Li, Huanzhi Mao, Qiuyang Mang, Hanchen Li, Joseph E. Gonzalez, and Alex Dimakis), the study shows that optimizing the stationary environment cuts token costs far more effectively than model swaps or prompt tweaks, without degrading task success.

Stationary environments in production

The paper focuses on what the authors call stationary environments.

In production deployments, agents rarely run in sterile single-turn sandboxes. They operate inside persistent environments shared across hundreds or thousands of tasks. A coding agent repeatedly navigates the same monolithic git repository. A support assistant searches the same corporate Slack workspace and ticketing platform. A data pipeline agent queries the same warehouse schemas.

The underlying artifacts in these environments stay relatively static, yet agents interact with them through raw, unoptimized interfaces.

To measure the impact of restructuring these spaces, the researchers built EnvOpt, a framework that uses an automated research agent to re-architect the environment representation for a given set of tasks. The optimizer restructures stored data, builds helper programs, generates local cheatsheets, and refines tool interfaces, testing changes against task performance without requiring human-labeled reference answers.

The resulting numbers on standard benchmarks challenge the standard playbook for reducing agent costs.

On AutomationBench, optimizing the stationary environment reduced the token cost of Claude Haiku 4.5 by 72.7 percent while raising its pass rate by 14.34 percent.

The optimization also transferred across model families. Deploying the same optimized environment to Claude Opus 5 reduced its operational cost by 68.1 percent with a 1.34 percent accuracy improvement.

When combined with harness optimization, the gains compounded. Stacking the optimized environment on top of Meta-Harness lowered Haiku 4.5 costs by a further 83.4 percent and added 11.17 percent accuracy over Meta-Harness alone. On Data-Eng-Bench, which evaluates agents on complex dbt data engineering tasks, the optimized environment reduced token expenses by 53.44 percent with zero loss in pass rate.

Where the token bill actually comes from

The authors tracked token consumption across input categories, output categories, tool calls, and environment feedback to pinpoint where the savings originated.

The results showed that the bulk of wasted spend does not come from model reasoning or final output generation. The largest token sink sits in environment feedback: the massive blocks of raw text, bloated JSON objects, and verbose error traces returned by exploratory tool calls.

When an agent needs to locate a ticket ID, find a function signature, or verify a schema, it issues exploratory queries. If the environment returns raw, unstructured dumps, the agent's context window inflates instantly. In subsequent turns, the model carries that accumulated noise forward, multiplying costs on every step.

The environment optimizations that produced the largest cost reductions shared a common pattern: they eliminated exploratory loops before the agent triggered them.

The most effective patterns were practical and straightforward:

  1. Pre-parsing messy payloads. On workspace automation tasks, helper scripts converted raw spreadsheets and multi-part emails into clean, plain-text summary blocks containing only the sender, subject, message ID, and relevant body chunks. The agent read clean text directly instead of burning tokens on repeated file-parsing tool invocations.

  2. Static API cheatsheets. Instead of requiring the agent to call discovery tools like api_search or api_fetch to understand endpoint parameters, the optimizer generated local text reference sheets for common Jira, Slack, and accounting actions. Having exact command structures available eliminated multi-turn trial calls.

  3. Filesystem index maps. In large file trees simulating enterprise workspaces, the optimizer compiled a single flat index file listing file paths, sizes, and file categories. The target agent could run a single grep command against the index instead of recursing through directories with find or ls.

  4. Local SQLite metadata caches. On data engineering benchmarks, the optimizer built an SQLite database indexing table definitions, upstream dependencies, and write destinations. Rather than reading dozens of dbt SQL models to trace lineage, the agent ran a single targeted SQL query.

The optimizations that failed

The paper also documents environment optimizations that failed during evaluation, and these failures offer useful warnings for production builders.

The first failure mode was the mega-file trap. In data engineering tasks, the research agent attempted to build a comprehensive reference file listing every possible value for every column across the database. The intention was to give the agent complete context in one place.

Instead, the massive file encouraged the target agent to make additional tool calls. Seeing a huge catalog of potential values caused the model to launch speculative exploration runs, ultimately increasing total token spend.

The second failure mode was imprecise search helpers. The optimizer built a custom search tool to help agents locate workspace documents. While the tool successfully identified relevant files, its ranking was too broad and included several adjacent files. Seeing those extra matches prompted the agent to read each one, driving up token consumption and execution time.

The third failure mode was rigid verification scripts. In repository debugging tasks, the optimizer introduced validation checks that rejected specific code patterns. While this saved time on early training tasks, it caused the agent to reject valid alternative patches on unseen problems, forcing it into costly recovery loops.

Engineering the workspace

The takeaway for software engineers building production agent workflows is clear.

When an agent gets expensive or unreliable, jumping immediately to fine-tuning or prompt rewrites is often the wrong first step. Look at the workspace you hand the agent. If the model has to run four shell commands just to discover which files matter, or parse a 400-line JSON payload to find two IDs, the environment is leaking tokens.

Structuring the environment with plain-text indexes, lightweight local SQLite caches, and clean CLI cheatsheets gives smaller models the footing they need to succeed at a fraction of the operating cost.

articles.title: What is your role in your agentic setup?
articles.description: A few weeks ago I wrote about how I stopped coding and started orchestrating. Ten terminal tabs,...
articles.body_html:
A few weeks ago I wrote about how I stopped coding and started orchestrating. Ten terminal tabs, three startups, me pressing Enter all day. Then I moved the whole setup to a Mac mini, put an orchestrator agent in charge of a pool of workers (coding agents, a design agent, a DevOps agent, an accounting agent), and went from 1 PR a day to 22.

I called myself an orchestrator. Then a manager of orchestrators. Both titles felt a bit grand for what I was actually doing.

With my daughter a couple of weeks away, I started re-reading my favorite book of Adler psychology, the courage to be happy. One idea stuck: the job of a parent is not to do things for the child, or to tell the child what to do all day. The job is to educate the child so that one day they can fend for themselves.

I read that sentence with my phone on my knee and the orchestrator asking me for the third time that morning whether it could run a migration.

And it clicked. I had the wrong job title all along.

You are not a product manager. You are an educator.

The industry has settled on two words for what humans do with AI agents: product manager and orchestrator. I think both are wrong, and the wrong word leads to the wrong setup.

A product manager writes a ticket, hands it over, and waits for the result. That is how I used my first workers. Every task started from zero. The agent didn't know my codebase conventions, didn't know we deploy with Kamal, and didn't know I hate service objects with more than one public method. So I wrote it all in the ticket. Every. Single. Time.

An orchestrator is worse. An orchestrator decides every move. That is the setup that turned me into a finger pressing Enter. The agents had no autonomy because I had given them none. I was not slow because the AI was slow; I was slow because I was the bottleneck in every decision.

An educator does something different. Adler is careful with the word: a teacher transmits facts; an educator shapes a person who can live on their own. An educator spends time up front so that later the child does not need them. You explain how the world works, you let them try, you correct, and you step back a bit more each time. The goal of the educator is to become unnecessary.

That is exactly what happened with my orchestrator without me noticing. It did not become useful because I gave it better tickets. It became useful because it knows how I work, what security I need, which decisions it can take alone and which ones to escalate to me. I educated it, mostly by accident.

Once I saw it as education, I started doing it on purpose.

Human knowledge, and AI knowledge

Adler makes a distinction I found useful. There is the knowledge you learn at school (maths, history, how to read), and there is a second kind of knowledge nobody writes an exam about: the shared rules for living with other people. You stop at a red light. You don’t talk in the cinema. You bring something when you are invited to dinner. Nobody is born with this. Every generation learns it from the previous one, and a child who does not learn it cannot function in society no matter how smart they are.

AI agents are in exactly that situation. The model is the smartest kid in the class. It knows Rails better than I do, it has read more Postgres documentation than any human alive. What it does not know is how to live in my house.

I started calling this AI knowledge: the basic set of rules an agent needs to perform tasks and fulfill its goals inside a specific environment. Not model weights, not prompts. The equivalent of knowing where the traffic lights are.

For my setup, AI knowledge looks like this:

Where things live: which repo is which startup, where the Obsidian vault is, which folder is the accounting drive.

How we ship: branch naming, PR size, what a green pipeline means, that nothing deploys on Friday evening Bali time.

What is dangerous: which commands need a human, which tables you never touch in production, what counts as a customer-facing change.

Who does what: the orchestrator dispatches, coding workers write and test, the design agent owns the UI, the DevOps agent deploys and monitors, the accounting agent does the books, I do strategy and the final say on money.

What already happened: decisions from co-founder meetings, bugs we already fixed last year, features we tried and killed.

None of this is in the model. All of it is in markdown files, a vault, and a handful of CLAUDE.md files that I keep adding to every time an agent does something that makes me say “no, not like that”.

The test is simple. If a brand new worker spins up tomorrow, can it fend for itself in my codebase with zero instructions from me? If the answer is no, I have not finished educating it. I have just written a very long ticket.

Knowledge only survives if it gets passed on

Human knowledge persists for one reason: people pass it forward. My parents taught me, I will teach my daughter; she will teach hers. Nobody re-derives the rules of society from scratch every morning.

Agents, by default, do exactly that. Every session starts from zero. Every worker is a newborn. Whatever a worker learned yesterday (that the test suite is flaky on the mailer specs, that the staging database has a weird extension) dies with its context window.

So the second part of the educator’s job is to make sure the knowledge outlives the one who learned it.

In practice, this means agents educating agents. Here is how it works in my setup:

A worker finishes a task and writes what it learned into the vault: a gotcha, a decision, a convention it discovered by breaking something.

The orchestrator reviews it. If it is a real rule and not a one-off, it goes into the shared AI knowledge. If it is noise, it gets dropped.

The next worker that touches that area reads it before starting.

I am not in that loop. That is the point. If I were the only channel through which knowledge moves between agents, I would be back to being the bottleneck, just with a nicer job title.

The nice side effect: when the orchestrator stops me from building a feature we already tried and killed last year, that is not the orchestrator being smart. That is a worker from eight months ago educating a worker from today, with me doing nothing.

What a well-educated agent looks like

Adler says a well-educated child has two things: they can take care of themselves, and they can live in harmony with others. I have found no better definition of a good agent.

1. Self-reliance

The agent can get from a task to a merged PR inside my environment without asking me anything. It knows where to look, how to run the tests, how to deploy, when to stop. The number I track for this is interruptions per task. When I started, it was 10 to 15 “allow this command?” per worker. Today the orchestrator absorbs almost all of them and escalates maybe one real decision a day to me.

This is also the one that lets me close the laptop. An agent that cannot fend for itself needs a human at the keyboard. An agent that can needs a Mac mini and a UPS.

2. Harmony with the environment

This is the one most people skip, and it is where agents do the most damage. A self-reliant agent with no sense of the environment is a toddler with a credit card. Very capable, very fast, zero awareness of what is around it.

Harmony means three things in my setup:

  1. Not recreating what already exists. The worker checks the vault and the codebase before writing a new service, a new helper, a new landing page section. The number of duplicated utility classes I had before this rule was embarrassing.

  2. Calling the right tool when needed. If there is a connector for Gmail, use it. If there is a script that generates invoices, run it, do not re-implement it in Ruby from scratch because you can. The right tool includes other agents: a coding worker that hits an accounting question hands it to the accounting agent; it does not improvise Singapore tax law. A worker that needs a new screen asks the design agent, it does not invent its own button style.

  3. Operating in sync with everyone else. Workers run in parallel. Thirty of them on a good night. One worker rewriting the User model while another one is adding a column to it is the agent version of two kids fighting over the same toy. The orchestrator’s job is to sequence them, and each worker’s job is to check what is in flight before it starts.

Self-reliance without harmony gives you fast chaos. Harmony without self-reliance gives you a polite agent that asks permission for everything. You need both, and you only get both by educating the agent, not by writing better tickets.

In Summary

If you take one thing from this post: stop asking “how do I write a better prompt” and start asking “what does this agent need to know to live here without me”.

Your role with AI is not product manager and not orchestrator. It is an educator, in Adler’s sense: someone whose job is to become unnecessary.

AI knowledge is the set of shared rules an agent needs to fend for itself in your environment. It lives in your repo and your vault, not in the model.

Knowledge persists better if agents pass it to other agents instead of simple .md files. If you are the only channel, you are the bottleneck.

A well-educated agent is self-reliant and in harmony with its environment. It does not rebuild what exists; it calls the right tool, and it stays in sync with the other agents.

Now, let’s educate.

Dani,

articles.title: I Stamped Every Row With DateTime.Now and Paid Twice
articles.description: DateTime.Now is DateTime.UtcNow plus a trip through your local time zone rules, and that trip isn't free in a hot loop. I counted: on a box with a real time zone it roughly doubles the cost of reading the clock.
articles.body_html:
I had a batch importer stamping DateTime.Now onto every row it processed. A few hundred thousand rows, one timestamp each, nothing I'd ever think twice about. Then I put a profiler on the thing because it was slower than it had any right to be, and there it was near the top: reading the clock. Not the database, not the parsing. The clock.

So I did the thing I always end up doing. I counted.

Now is UtcNow wearing a coat

DateTime.Now doesn't read a "local clock." There's no such thing. It reads UTC, exactly like DateTime.UtcNow does, and then converts that instant into local time using TimeZoneInfo.Local. That conversion is the whole difference between the two calls. One reads the clock. The other reads the clock and then asks the time zone database what your offset is right now, DST and all.

The offset lookup is the part that costs. And here's the bit that surprised me: it costs even when the answer is zero.

Putting a clock on the clock

I read each one 20 million times, summed the ticks so nothing got optimized away, best of five rounds. Same loop, three bodies.

static long ReadUtcNow() => DateTime.UtcNow.Ticks;
static long ReadNow()    => DateTime.Now.Ticks;
static long ReadStopwatch() => Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();

First run, on the container as it ships, which pins itself to UTC:

Local time zone: Etc/UTC

20,000,000 reads, best of 5
  DateTime.UtcNow     661.5 ms     33.1 ns/call
  DateTime.Now        911.8 ms     45.6 ns/call
  Now / UtcNow         1.38x

A UTC box has a zero offset. There's nothing to add. And Now is still almost 40% slower, because it does the lookup to find out the offset is zero. The work happens whether or not it changes the answer.

Then I pointed TZ at a real zone, the kind your laptop or an on-prem server actually runs, with daylight saving rules to evaluate:

Local time zone: America/New_York

20,000,000 reads, best of 5
  DateTime.UtcNow     678.3 ms     33.9 ns/call
  DateTime.Now      1,357.2 ms     67.9 ns/call
  Now / UtcNow         2.00x

Twice the cost. UtcNow sits around 33 ns no matter what I do; Now lands somewhere between 60 and 68 ns across runs. The time zone isn't part of reading the clock. It's a question Now asks afterward, every single time.

This is a container, not a lab, so I care about the ratio, not the exact nanoseconds. The ratio was steady run to run. Roughly double on a real zone, roughly a third extra on UTC.

The tool I actually wanted

Half the time I reach for DateTime.Now I'm not even recording a wall-clock time. I'm measuring how long something took. For that, both Now and UtcNow are the wrong tool, because they drag calendar math into a job that's really just "count ticks between here and there." Stopwatch does exactly that and nothing else:

  Stopwatch.GetTimestamp   637.3 ms     31.9 ns/call

Cheapest of the three, and it never touches a time zone or even cares what day it is. If you're timing a block of code, this is the one.

When I'd leave it alone

If you call DateTime.Now a handful of times per request, this whole post is noise. Thirty-odd extra nanoseconds disappears against literally anything else your code does. I'm not going to rewrite a login handler to shave that off, and neither should you. The importer only cared because it was reading the clock once per row, hundreds of thousands of times, in a loop that otherwise did very little. Hot path, high count. That's the only place it shows up.

And don't go blindly swapping Now for UtcNow in display code. If you're formatting a timestamp a human is going to read, they want their local time, and UtcNow will happily show them the wrong hour. That's a correctness bug, and no benchmark makes it worth shipping.

My own rule, for what it's worth: compute and store in UTC, read the clock with UtcNow, time things with Stopwatch, and convert to local exactly once, at the edge, right before a person sees it. Local time is a presentation concern. Treating it like a data concern is how you end up paying the time zone tax a few hundred thousand times to import a file nobody's even looking at yet.

Here's the whole thing if you want to run it yourself. New console project targeting net10.0, drop this in Program.cs, then dotnet run -c Release, and TZ="America/New_York" dotnet run -c Release for the wider gap:

using System.Diagnostics;

Console.WriteLine($"Local time zone: {TimeZoneInfo.Local.Id}");

const int Iterations = 20_000_000;
const int Rounds = 5;

// Warm up both paths so the JIT and the time-zone cache are hot.
_ = Measure(ReadUtcNow, 1_000_000);
_ = Measure(ReadNow, 1_000_000);

long utcTicks = long.MaxValue, nowTicks = long.MaxValue, swTicks = long.MaxValue;
for (int r = 0; r < Rounds; r++)
{
    utcTicks = Math.Min(utcTicks, Measure(ReadUtcNow, Iterations));
    nowTicks = Math.Min(nowTicks, Measure(ReadNow, Iterations));
    swTicks  = Math.Min(swTicks,  Measure(ReadStopwatch, Iterations));
}

double utcMs = utcTicks * 1000.0 / Stopwatch.Frequency;
double nowMs = nowTicks * 1000.0 / Stopwatch.Frequency;
double swMs  = swTicks  * 1000.0 / Stopwatch.Frequency;

Console.WriteLine($"{Iterations:N0} reads, best of {Rounds}");
Console.WriteLine($"  DateTime.UtcNow        {utcMs,8:N1} ms   {utcMs * 1e6 / Iterations,5:N1} ns/call");
Console.WriteLine($"  DateTime.Now           {nowMs,8:N1} ms   {nowMs * 1e6 / Iterations,5:N1} ns/call");
Console.WriteLine($"  Now / UtcNow           {nowMs / utcMs,8:N2}x");
Console.WriteLine($"  Stopwatch.GetTimestamp {swMs,8:N1} ms   {swMs * 1e6 / Iterations,5:N1} ns/call");

return;

static long Measure(Func<long> body, int iterations)
{
    long sink = 0;
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++)
        sink += body();
    sw.Stop();
    if (sink == -1) Console.WriteLine("unreachable"); // keep the loop alive
    return sw.ElapsedTicks;
}

static long ReadUtcNow() => DateTime.UtcNow.Ticks;
static long ReadNow() => DateTime.Now.Ticks;
static long ReadStopwatch() => Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();

Do you default to Now or UtcNow when you're not thinking about it? I'd bet most of us type whichever one our fingers learned first. Curious which camp you're in.

— still putting clocks on things nobody asked me to time

articles.title: I Expected a 100x JSON Slowdown. I Got 1.9x.
articles.description: I benchmarked the old 'never build a new JsonSerializerOptions per call' rule on .NET 10, expecting the famous 100x penalty. I got 1.9x. Here's why the runtime now rescues you, and the one case where it still doesn't.
articles.body_html:
I had a little serialize helper that sailed through code review. It looked like this: return JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, new JsonSerializerOptions { ... }). A fresh options object, built right there in the method, on every call. Every post I'd ever half-read told me this was a cardinal sin, the kind that turns a fast endpoint slow and earns you a 100x regression. So I braced for the worst, wrote a benchmark, and went hunting for the catastrophe.

I didn't find it. On the path my code actually took, I got 1.9x. That was surprising enough that I kept pulling the thread, and the real answer turned out to be more useful than the scary one.

The three ways to get options wrong (and right)

Here's the payload. A small order, the kind of thing a handler serializes thousands of times a second.

record Order(Guid Id, string Customer, DateTime PlacedAtUtc, LineItem[] Items, string? Note);
record LineItem(string Name, int Quantity, decimal UnitPrice);

And here are the three ways I serialized it. Case A is the fix everyone recommends: build the options once, reuse the instance.

// A — one shared instance, reused everywhere.
var shared = new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull
};
string SerializeShared(Order o) => JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, shared);

Case B is my sin: a new instance every call, but with the exact same configuration each time. This is what the accidental version almost always looks like in real code.

// B — new instance each call, identical config.
static string SerializeNewSameConfig(Order o)
{
    var options = new JsonSerializerOptions
    {
        PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
        DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull
    };
    return JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, options);
}

Case C is the one I didn't write but easily could have: a new instance each call where the configuration also changes. Here I just nudge MaxDepth to make every instance distinct, but in the wild this is what you get when options are assembled from per-request data.

// C — new instance each call, config varies.
static string SerializeNewVaryingConfig(Order o, int i)
{
    var options = new JsonSerializerOptions
    {
        PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
        DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull,
        MaxDepth = 32 + (i & 63) // harmless, but makes every instance distinct
    };
    return JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, options);
}

The measurement is boring on purpose: warm up a thousand times so the JIT and first-use caches aren't in the number, collect garbage, then time 200,000 serializations and take the best of five rounds. I also grab GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() around the loop so I can see the allocations, not just the clock.

static (double ms, long bytes) Measure(Func<Order, string> fn, Order o, int iterations)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) _ = fn(o);
    GC.Collect(); GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers(); GC.Collect();

    long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++) _ = fn(o);
    sw.Stop();
    return (sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds, GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before);
}

What came out

This isn't a lab. It's a 2-core container on .NET 10, best-of-five, and I care about the ratios, not the absolute milliseconds.

Iterations per run: 200,000

A shared instance        :     153.7 ms      186.2 MB
B new, same config       :     295.6 ms      224.7 MB
C new, varying config    :     593.9 ms      329.5 MB

B vs A :    1.9x time     1.2x alloc
C vs A :    3.9x time     1.8x alloc

So my supposedly-criminal Case B costs about 1.9x the time and 1.2x the memory. Real, worth fixing, but nowhere near the horror story.

Why B isn't the disaster the internet promised

The reason is something JsonSerializerOptions does behind your back. The expensive part of serialization isn't the writing. It's building the metadata that describes how to walk your type (JsonTypeInfo for Order, LineItem, and every property). Years ago, each options instance built and cached that metadata on itself, so a new instance per call meant rebuilding the whole thing every single time. That's where the 100x stories came from.

Modern .NET keeps a cache keyed on the options configuration, not just the instance. When I create a new options object with the same settings as one it's already seen, the runtime recognizes the configuration and reuses the metadata it built before. I still pay to allocate the object and do the equivalence lookup every call, which is the 1.9x, but I don't pay to rebuild the metadata, the part that used to hurt.

Case C is where that safety net has a hole. Every instance there has a different MaxDepth, so the configuration never matches and the cache can't help. Close to 4x and climbing. The lesson isn't that new is fine now. The penalty scales with how different your options are, and a per-call object is one small refactor away from becoming the per-request-varying kind.

What I actually do

I still make it static readonly and reuse it. Not because 1.9x scares me. On a background job that serializes once an hour I genuinely would not care, and you shouldn't either. I do it because a new JsonSerializerOptions sitting inside a hot method is a smell. It's the thing that looks innocent until someone adds options.Converters.Add(somethingFromTheRequest) six months later and tips you into Case C. Reusing one instance closes that door before anyone can walk through it.

If you want to confirm the shape on your own hardware, here's the full runnable program, a net10.0 console project. Drop it in Program.cs and dotnet run -c Release. (My usual repo push got blocked by a sandbox permission hiccup this run, so you get the whole thing right here instead of a link.)

using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Text.Json;
using System.Text.Json.Serialization;

var order = new Order(
    Guid.Parse("8a1f6c2e-0b3d-4e5a-9c7f-112233445566"),
    "Acme Robotics",
    new DateTime(2026, 11, 6, 7, 10, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc),
    [ new("Servo motor", 4, 23.50m), new("Control board", 1, 189.00m), new("Cable harness", 2, 7.25m) ],
    "Leave at the loading dock");

const int Iterations = 200_000;

var shared = new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull
};
string A(Order o, int i) => JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, shared);

static string B(Order o, int i) => JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull
});

static string C(Order o, int i) => JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull,
    MaxDepth = 32 + (i & 63)
});

static (double ms, long bytes) Measure(Func<Order, int, string> fn, Order o, int n)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) _ = fn(o, i);
    GC.Collect(); GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers(); GC.Collect();
    long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) _ = fn(o, i);
    sw.Stop();
    return (sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds, GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before);
}

static (double ms, long bytes) BestOf(Func<Order, int, string> fn, Order o, int n, int rounds)
{
    double best = double.MaxValue; long bytes = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < rounds; r++)
    {
        var (ms, b) = Measure(fn, o, n);
        if (ms < best) { best = ms; bytes = b; }
    }
    return (best, bytes);
}

var a = BestOf(A, order, Iterations, 5);
var b = BestOf(B, order, Iterations, 5);
var c = BestOf(C, order, Iterations, 5);

Console.WriteLine($"Iterations per run: {Iterations:N0}\n");
