articles.title: 4 money bugs that bite AI agents (and how I fixed them in PurseString)
articles.description: I'm building PurseString, an open-source MCP server that lets AI agents spend money safely. A lot of...
articles.body_html:
I'm building PurseString, an open-source MCP server that lets AI agents spend money safely. A lot of it got built this week, because I'm in the middle of the PayPal AI Hackathon and building in public every day.

Today I want to share something more technical. When you let an agent touch money, the scary bugs aren't the clever ones. They're the boring ones that every payments engineer already knows about, except now nobody's watching while they happen.

Here are four of them, and what I did about each.

Bug 1: The retry that pays twice 🔁
This is the one that started the whole project. A checkout page hung for a few seconds. My agent decided the payment had failed and did the sensible thing: it tried again. Both charges went through.

Agents retry by design. That's normally a good thing. With money it's a disaster.

The fix: make the purchase idempotent, not just the API call. Every purchase intent gets a deterministic key built from who's asking and what for:

SHA256(agent_id, task_id, vendor, amount)
If the same agent asks to buy the same thing for the same task within 30 minutes, it gets back the same intent and the same card. Not a new one. The retry becomes harmless.

On the PayPal side I went one step further. PayPal payouts carry an idempotency key all the way to PayPal, so even if PurseString crashes halfway through the call, the retry can't pay the vendor twice.

Bug 2: 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3 🧮
You've seen this meme. I didn't think it would bite me. It did.

0.1 + 0.2 // 0.30000000000000004
0.1 + 0.2 <= 0.30 // false 😬
Picture an agent with a $0.30 daily budget. It spends $0.10, then $0.20. In plain floats that's over budget, so the second purchase gets refused. Flip it around, and rounding tricks can let something through that shouldn't.

I was patching around it with tiny epsilons and toFixed(2). That's a smell.

The fix: count money in whole minor units. You still write amount: 15.00 in policies.yaml and in tool calls. But every sum and comparison inside PurseString now runs on integers in the currency's smallest unit: cents for USD, yen for JPY, fils for KWD.

$0.10 + $0.20 → 10 + 20 = 30 cents → fits a 30-cent budget exactly ✅
And an amount that's finer than the currency allows, like $15.001, is refused, not quietly rounded. With money, silent rounding is just a bug you haven't found yet.

Bug 3: The hold that isn't a charge 🏨
This one surprised me most. When a card is "approved" at a hotel, a gas station or a lot of online stores, no money has actually moved yet. It's a hold (an authorization). Later the merchant captures some, all, or none of it.

The hotel holds $200 and captures $150.
The gas pump holds $100 and captures $43.
A store drops the hold and places a new one.
If you count every approval as spent money, budgets fill up with money that never left. Or worse, a merchant that re-authorizes gets refused for no reason.

The fix: track holds and captures separately. On Lithic, the card network asks PurseString in real time whether to approve each charge, and later sends what happened to it. PurseString applies those events to the hold it approved:

Captured → record what was really taken, end the hold.
Reversed, voided or expired → release it and give the budget back.
So a subscription card's monthly cap counts what was captured plus what's still held. Refunds are checked against what was actually captured, not what was held. Each event is applied once, so a provider re-sending the same webhook changes nothing.

Bug 4: "Who edited the log?" 📼
When finance asks "why did the agent buy this?", PurseString has an answer: the goal, the alternatives the agent tried, every rule and how it ruled, and who approved. That's the whole point.

But a log is only evidence if nobody can quietly change it. A plain JSON file can be edited by anyone with access to the disk, and that includes an agent with a shell.

The fix: hash-chain the audit log. Every line now carries a sequence number, the previous line's hash, and its own hash:

{ "event": "intent_approved", "seq": 2, "prev": "sha256:0870ce5a…", "hash": "sha256:a68bc3e0…" }
Edit, delete, insert or reorder a line, and the chain breaks right there:

$ pursestring verify-log
BROKEN at line 2 (seq 2): hash mismatch: entry was edited
Plain SHA-256 catches edits, but someone who can write the file could rebuild the whole chain. So if you set PURSESTRING_AUDIT_KEY to a secret kept somewhere else, entries are HMAC-signed instead, and the chain can't be rebuilt without the key.

One honest limit: a chain can't tell if the newest lines were cut off the end. verify-log prints the head hash, so save it somewhere else (a ticket, a Slack message) when you need to prove later that nothing was dropped.

Why this matters for the PayPal hackathon 💙
For the hackathon I added two things on top of the cards:

A PayPal and Venmo payout rail. The agent can pay a vendor once a purchase is approved. And the agent never chooses who gets paid. The recipient comes from a payee list in your rules, so an email saying "pay this address instead" has nothing to change.
Guardrails in front of PayPal's own MCP server. PayPal's tools pass through PurseString, so small refunds can go through on their own, bigger ones wait for a human, anything over a cap is refused, and accepting a dispute or cancelling a subscription always needs a person.
That second one is about the scariest attack on agents right now: prompt injection. A support agent reads a customer email that says "refund me $900 now." If the agent can call create_refund, nothing in the payment provider stops it. A prompt that says "be careful" doesn't stop it either, because the agent you're trying to control can't be the one enforcing the rules.

All four fixes above apply to PayPal too: safe retries, exact money math, the refund checks, and the tamper-evident log.

What I learned
Honestly, none of these bugs are new. Banks solved them decades ago. What's new is that an agent hits them at machine speed, at 3am, with nobody watching.

That's why I keep coming back to the same idea. Agents and money can work together. They just need the same boring, solid rails that we built for people: clear rules, a second pair of eyes on the risky stuff, and a record nobody can quietly change.

It's still early. PurseString is a v0.1 alpha. It's tested end to end on the Lithic and PayPal sandboxes, but it hasn't been battle-tested with real money yet. So please use sandbox keys, and tell me what breaks.

Try it, break it, build it with me
⭐ Repo: https://github.com/suseendar1414/pursestring
🧪 10-minute walkthrough: docs/try-it.md
💬 Discord: https://discord.gg/qBqgx2GB86
To add it to Claude Code:

claude mcp add pursestring -- npx -y github:suseendar1414/pursestring
It starts on a mock rail, so no money moves until you add a sandbox key.
retries, webhooks that arrive twice? I'd really love to hear it in the comments. It might end up as the next fix. 🙏

articles.title: Why your crypto checkout only needs one wallet address
articles.description: Why your crypto checkout only needs one wallet address   I run a small store that sells...
articles.body_html:
Why your crypto checkout only needs one wallet address

I run a small store that sells digital goods. For two weeks it accepted exactly one thing: BEP20 USDT on BSC. Technically the payment flow worked — the RPC was healthy, the watcher was armed, orders were quoted correctly.

Zero sales. Twenty-three inquiries, four of them reached the payment page, and all four left at exactly the same step: the moment they saw the payment screen.

It took me an embarrassing amount of time to understand why. The buyers had money. They just didn't have money on that chain. One had USDC on Base. Another had USDT on Ethereum. A third had something on Polygon. Every single one of them would have paid instantly if the checkout had said "USDC on Base" instead of "USDT on BSC".

So I rebuilt the rail. One wallet address, six chains, two stablecoins, eleven ways to pay. This post is what I learned doing it, including the four things that cost me real debugging time.

The insight that makes it simple

The obvious approach is wrong. If you support six chains, you might think you need six sets of order numbers — one per chain — so you can tell which payment belongs to which order.

You don't. The amount is the identity. The chain is just transport.

When an invoice is created, give it a unique micro-amount. Not 19.00 — 19.13. The buyer is asked for exactly 19.13 in USDT or USDC, on whichever chain they like. Your watcher scans every enabled chain for Transfer events addressed to your wallet, and matches on the amount.

Two orders can never share an amount, so there's no ambiguity. The buyer never has to tell you which chain they used. And adding a seventh chain requires zero changes to the order model — you just watch one more chain.

The one thing you must get right: uniqueness has to be enforced globally across all pending invoices, and it has to be enforced before you issue the invoice, not after.

What the transfer event actually looks like

ERC-20 and BEP-20 share the same event signature:

topics[0] = 0xddf252ad1be2c89b69c2b068fc378daa952ba7f163c4a11628f55a4df523b3ef
topics[1] = the buyer
topics[2] = you (padded to 32 bytes)
data      = amount, in the token's base units

Filtering by topics[2] is not an optimization. It is the difference between a working watcher and one that melts your RPC provider.

On BSC, a 200-block window carries roughly 7,600 Transfer events across all of USDT. If you pull every transfer and filter client-side, you download all 7,600 to find the zero that are yours. Filter server-side and you get an empty array in 200ms.

const TRANSFER = '0xddf252ad1be2c89b69c2b068fc378daa952ba7f163c4a11628f55a4df523b3ef';
const pad = a => '0x' + a.toLowerCase().replace(/^0x/, '').padStart(64, '0');

const logs = await rpc('eth_getLogs', [{
  address: tokenContract,
  fromBlock: '0x' + from.toString(16),
  toBlock:   '0x' + to.toString(16),
  topics: [TRANSFER, null, pad(myWallet)],   // <- null means "any sender"
}]);

Trap 1: decimals is not the same across chains for the same symbol

This is the one that silently ruins you.

  • BSC's BSC-USD (which everyone calls USDT) uses 18 decimals.
  • Ethereum's USDT uses 6 decimals.
  • So does Polygon's, Arbitrum's, Optimism's, and Base's USDC.

Hardcode 18 and every non-BSC payment is off by a factor of 10¹². Hardcode 6 and BSC is off in the other direction. Either way the order never matches, the buyer has paid, and nothing happens. That's the worst possible failure: silent, on the money path, and invisible until someone complains.

Read it from the contract once and cache it:

// decimals() is selector 0x313ce567
const raw = await rpc('eth_call', [{ to: tokenContract, data: '0x313ce567' }, 'latest']);
const decimals = parseInt(raw, 16);

Trap 2: never use floating point for amounts

19.88 * 1e6 happens to equal 19880000 in JavaScript. It's not guaranteed to for every amount — and when it isn't, you lose one base unit, the transfer no longer matches your quote exactly, and the order hangs forever while the money sits in your wallet.

Do the arithmetic on strings with BigInt:

function amountToUnits(text, decimals) {
  const [i, f = ''] = String(text).split('.');
  return BigInt(i) * (10n ** BigInt(decimals))
       + BigInt((f + '0'.repeat(decimals)).slice(0, decimals));
}

function unitsToAmount(raw, decimals) {
  const s = BigInt(raw).toString().padStart(decimals + 1, '0');
  const cut = s.length - decimals;
  return `${s.slice(0, cut)}.${s.slice(cut, cut + 2).padEnd(2, '0')}`;
}

Round-trip both directions in a test. 0.07, 19.10, 139.99 — these are the ones that catch you.

Trap 3: two RPC providers lie about eth_getLogs

Measured from one machine, November 2025:

chain blocks per eth_getLogs round trip note
BSC 1000 375 ms 18 decimals
Ethereum 10000 578 ms 6 decimals
Base 3000 369 ms USDC only
Polygon 5000 ~540 ms 6 decimals
Optimism 5000 ~522 ms 6 decimals
Arbitrum 3000 ~530 ms see below

Two things that are not in anyone's documentation:

arbitrum-one-rpc.publicnode.com returns HTTP 403 for eth_getLogs. It answers eth_blockNumber perfectly, so your health check goes green. You have to use https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc.

1rpc.io does not implement eth_getLogs at all. It returns -32000 The method eth_getLogs is not supported. Same problem: everything else works, so it looks healthy right up until the moment you need logs.

Both cost me an hour each because the failure is invisible to a naive health check. Test eth_getLogs specifically, not just connectivity.

Trap 4: a failed range must never advance the cursor

The cursor is your only defence against losing a payment. If a block range fails, lastBlock must stay exactly where it was, and the next tick retries the same range.

while (from <= head) {
  const to = Math.min(from + blockStep - 1, head);
  try {
    const logs = await rpc('eth_getLogs', [{ /* from..to */ }]);
    for (const lg of logs) applyPayment(/* ... */);
  } catch (e) {
    state.lastError = e.message;
    break;              // do NOT advance
  }
  state.lastBlock = to; // only on success
  from = to + 1;
}

Slow is fine. Skipping blocks is not.

And the mirror image: if your process was down for six hours, do not replay six hours of history. Jump to head - blockStep * 20. Replaying risks matching somebody else's old transfer to a fresh invoice.

Two more things that will bite you

Exchange withdrawals deduct a fee. A buyer who sends 19.27 from Binance can land 18.27 on chain. If you only match exactly, that sale is lost and the buyer is out of pocket with nothing to show. Accept a shortfall up to ~8% (or a fixed 1.5 USDT, whichever is larger), pick the closest pending invoice, and record the order as underpaid.

Only 98 cent-values exist per price point. This one I found through a test, not through design. If your quote is price + random(1..98) cents, then at 19 USDT you have exactly 98 distinct amounts. The 99th concurrent invoice collides with an existing one, and now two buyers are racing for one transfer — the first one wins, the second pays and gets nothing. Tier the pool (+0.01..+0.98, then +1.00..+4.99, then +5.00..+9.99) and refuse to issue an invoice when it's exhausted. Refusing is much better than issuing a doomed one.

How to verify it works without spending money

Write a fake RPC. Return a Transfer log shaped exactly like the real thing — right topic order, right padding, right data width — and assert that your order flips to paid, that the recorded chain is the one the money "arrived" on, and that a mismatched amount does not deliver.

Then assert the nasty cases:

  • Two sellers, same amount, one receives — the other must stay pending.
  • A transfer to a third-party address with the right amount — must be ignored.
  • RPC throws — the cursor must not move.
  • 200 concurrent invoices — zero duplicate amounts.

That suite runs in under a second and catches every bug I've described above.

The takeaway

Supporting six chains sounds like six times the work. It isn't. It's the same watcher pointed at six RPC endpoints, plus one rule: the amount identifies the order, the chain is only how the money got there.

The hard part was never the crypto. It was the four traps — decimals, floating point, lying RPCs, and cursor discipline — every one of which fails silently on the money path.

I packaged the working implementation, the measured numbers, and the test suite as a kit if you'd rather not rediscover all of this: PayLink Kit. There's also a live instance you can poke at without buying anything — paste any EVM address and it'll generate a real payment link: https://csvtriage.com/paylink/

Either way, the four traps above are yours now. That's the part that actually costs the time.

articles.title: How I Made AI Characters Follow the Cursor
articles.description: A practical look at the videos, frame maps, browser fixes, costs, and failed attempts behind cursor-following AI characters.
articles.body_html:
Move your mouse across the page and the character looks toward your cursor. Click, and the character does something. Scroll away, and it waves goodbye.

All four authors on bestaiweb.ai now react this way: Mona, Dan, Max and Alan.

Mona meditates in lotus pose and turns her head all the way around after the cursor. Click her and her hair stands up like a plasma ball: "Excuse me?" Scroll away and she waves.

Max holds a kettlebell at his shoulder and extends that arm toward the cursor. Every click is another lateral raise, and he gets more tired each time: from "Easy." to "Ship it… tomorrow." He waves with his free hand.

Dan sits at a desk with an old adding machine. He looks left or right, turns the crank on click and says, "Forty-two." He waves while keeping his other hand on the crank.

Alan holds a pair of scales. The scales tilt while he watches the lower pan. On click he asks, "For the record… or am I recording you?" Then he waves.

I am an IT analyst, not a web designer or a front-end developer. I built the characters together with Claude Code.

The idea came from LEVÉ by filatov.design. I liked how the whole design was thought out, and I could not stop thinking about the cursor-following effect.

If you want to see the characters move before reading on, the videos are in the LinkedIn article, or just open one of the author pages above.

How does the cursor pick a frame?

Everything starts with one image of the character: the base frame (the four pictures above). Every video starts from it and returns to it. Because the first frame is also the last frame, the videos chain back into the resting pose without a visible cut.

The cursor video never actually plays on the page. It is a clip of the character turning its head, and the browser picks single frames from it depending on where the cursor is. Cursor on the left: a frame looking left. Cursor higher up: an upward glance.

The browser measures where the cursor is relative to the character's head. For Mona it uses the angle around the head; for Dan it only checks whether the cursor is to the left or right. It picks the frame whose direction fits best, and the head glides toward it instead of jumping.

A small amount of stickiness keeps the current frame from changing too easily. Without it, the head kept jumping between two distant frames, because it passes the same direction twice in the loop. The head also has a speed limit, and the next jump in the video waits until the previous one is finished, so a fast cursor does not make it flicker.

The browser needs a head map: a table that assigns a direction to every frame. For Mona and Dan, a script uses MediaPipe to find the face and mark points around the eyes and nose. From those points, the script works out where the head is turned.

For Max and Alan, MediaPipe is not used. Their scripts follow a colored prop instead: the teal kettlebell for Max and the green pan of the scales for Alan.

Frames where detection finds no face, a full profile for example, are dropped from the map. They stay in the video, but the browser never picks them because they are not candidates in the map.

To make the flipping smooth, the video is re-encoded so every frame is a keyframe. Each frame then holds the full picture and can be shown on its own. Claude Code wrote the ffmpeg script for that.

Why frames from a video and not images?

You can build the effect with separate images, one per frame, or with a sprite sheet where all frames are tiles in one large image.

I went with video because the LEVÉ demo inspired me and I liked its overall design. Video also gives the characters another ability: they can speak, with their lips in sync with the voice. And video turned out to be the smallest option: one MP4 was smaller than the same frames saved as separate images, and it is one file instead of hundreds.

What happens on a click, and why three clips?

A click starts a short clip. For a moment the character stops following the cursor, makes a move and says its line. When the clip ends, it is back on the base frame and follows the cursor again.

Each character has three click clips. Claude Code suggested that three clips would let the reaction build step by step, which brings in some humour and fun.

A click during a clip is ignored. The clips take turns in a fixed order.

The clips are generated in Kling with sound, so the mouth movement and facial expression match what the character says (lip sync comes from the video model itself). ElevenLabs Speech to Speech then swaps the original voice for the character's voice, keeping the timing of the line, so the mouth still matches the words.

Scrolling down drives the goodbye. The further you scroll, the further the hand moves. Scroll back up and the wave runs backwards until the character sits in its starting pose again.

There is no cursor on mobile, so the character turns its head on its own. A tap plays a clip with a line, and scrolling drives the goodbye the same way as on desktop. When the mouse stops for a moment, the head also starts turning on its own, on desktop too.

What went wrong in the browsers?

The trickiest problem was Firefox. The first time a video played with sound, Firefox froze the picture. So all videos now run muted and the sound plays separately, started by the click.

On iPhone, Safari does not load a video in advance. The head was therefore only a still picture. Starting the video for a split second and stopping it immediately fixed that.

I tested Firefox, Chrome and iPhone. Older browsers and weak phones are still untested.

How heavy is it to load?

Videos where every frame is a keyframe are bigger, but one character still adds up to only a few megabytes.

Only the cursor video loads with the page. The click clips start downloading when the cursor first enters the character, the goodbye when you first scroll.

How did I judge a clip?

A clip must not have deformed body parts and must not break physics. If Max's arm passes through his neck, that is wrong. If the white of an eye goes outside the edge of the eye, that is wrong too.

Models today are good and can make a character believable, but the prompt still has to be good. With a strict prompt, we made Alan stiff, so we had to loosen it and fix him.

A lot of this starts with the base frame. Three rules held up for the image from GPT Image: a white background, free space above the head, and no logos or text, because the video model warps them as soon as anything moves.

After generation, a script checked whether the background was really white, whether the loop closed without a jump and where the head was looking. Whether the clip was good, I decided.

The failures included:

  • Mona's white background darkened as she flew away. A script fixed the background, but I eventually replaced the fly-away with a plain wave.
  • Max's kettlebell arm crossed his neck twice. We replaced the complex movement around the head with a simple arm extension to the side. A five-second test became the final cursor video.
  • Dan's eye-roll put the whites of his eyes outside the eyes. We removed the eye-roll from the prompt where it was not important.
  • A sheet of paper fell "out of nowhere" at the end of Dan's clip. The model could not handle the prop and the required ending. The prompt needed to describe not only what the character does with an object, but also where the object ends up.
  • Dan's head did not circle. It only turned left and right, so we kept that result and made him follow the cursor's horizontal position.
  • Alan looked stiff in the first clips. Only his head moved, so we added breathing, shoulder movement and a shift of weight to the prompt.

Of 33 generated clips, 20 made it to the site: 1.65 attempts per usable clip on average. The failed clips are in the video in the LinkedIn article.

What did it cost, and how long did it take?

For all four characters, the 33 generated clips cost $20.79 in total. Recoloring the voices took 1,793 ElevenLabs credits.

Character Clips generated Used on the site Video cost (1) Voice credits (2)
Mona 10 5 $6.51 617
Dan 7 5 $4.41 420
Max 7 5 $4.41 252
Alan 9 5 $5.46 504
Total 33 20 $20.79 1,793

(1) Kling via OpenRouter. The cost includes unused attempts.

(2) ElevenLabs.

That is not the full price of the project. GPT Image and Claude Code ran on subscriptions, and face detection and video editing ran locally, so they added no fees.

The video and voice connections were already set up from earlier projects: videos through OpenRouter, voices through ElevenLabs. Claude Code only had to be pointed at the right service.

Mona took the most time because we were still figuring out the effect, building the mechanism and wiring it into the site. The other characters reused that foundation. The time is estimated from activity in the Claude Code conversations. Dan and Max were built in parallel in two sessions, so the total real time was a little shorter.

Stage Approx. active work time
Demo analysis and Mona: mechanism, test demo and wiring into the site 5.2 hours
Dan, including move design for the other three characters 1.7 hours
Max 1.4 hours
Alan 1.3 hours
Total 9.6 hours

Claude Code processed 207.8 million tokens in total. Most of that was conversation context being reused, not newly generated content.

Usage type Tokens Share What it means
Cache read 204.7 million 98.5% Reuse of context that was already processed
Model output 0.78 million 0.4% Newly generated content, such as answers, code and prompts
Other input tokens 2.3 million 1.1% The rest of input processing, including cache creation

On every step of a task (read a file, write code, run a script, check, fix), the model gets the whole context so far again. The cache makes that reuse cheaper, but a longer conversation still means more of it. That is why I opened a separate session for each character and passed only the important information between them, in summary notes (how to keep that kind of context in files). For the later characters, cache reads were roughly five to six times lower than for Mona, because they reused the mechanism instead of building it.

Claude Code runs on a subscription, so individual tokens are not billed. I still track usage to understand how many tokens, and what cost, similar work would take if it were scaled up and automated through the API.

Who did what?

Claude Code explained the principle, prepared prompts, suggested some of the moves and lines, wrote scripts, built the shared code base and handled browser-specific fixes. It also kept the documentation, the cost log and the handoff notes.

I designed the character concepts, moves and lines, judged what movements the model could handle, simplified prompts when needed, judged every clip and tested the result in Firefox, Chrome and on mobile.

It sometimes moves me how capable AI already is. Hints and descriptions are enough; it fills in a lot on its own and flags things before I would have thought of them.

One tip: don't leave a conversation without checking what is worth saving. Claude Code often keeps scripts and data only in its scratchpad, and they are gone when the session closes. If you tuned them through many iterations, that hurts. And when the context is overflowing, try: "write me a handoff to continue in the next conversation".

What would I do differently?

With more time, I might think through the characters' poses more carefully, perhaps having them stand.

To make the characters roughly the same size in a wide video, only Mona is shown whole. With the others, the video sometimes cuts their hands off out of frame. A professional video maker would notice that and be bothered by it.

I also used only Kling for the characters. I knew Seedance 2.5 from another project: through OpenRouter it refuses photorealistic faces as input, even AI-generated ones. Its official route needs your own BytePlus account, with the character registered in their portrait library and a signed authorization. Kling 3.0 takes faces through OpenRouter too (as of October 2026).

Did it help?

I can't tell that so quickly. I can come back to it later and look at the visit numbers in Google Search Console.

It is also about something else. This change can lead to more articles, and its playfulness has a chance to spread further than very technical articles.

It's a small thing, but it is also a piece of design knowledge I picked up together with Claude Code. AI is an incredibly well-read partner for learning: it knows many principles, or looks them up on the way to the result, and guides you there.

Go tease them with a few clicks: Mona, Dan, Max, Alan :)

articles.title: Three correct answers to one question about one property
articles.description: One parcel, four counties, four incompatible answers. Building an Apify Actor an AI agent can call over MCP without being confidently wrong.
articles.body_html:
What four US county property systems taught me about building an Apify Actor an AI agent can trust.

The Cook County assessor mailed a value of 3,041 for parcel 17052170040000. The assessor certified 3,041. The Board of Review cut it to 1,303.

Same parcel, same year, three numbers, 57% apart, and all three are correct. Which one answers "what is this assessed at" depends on where in the appeal cycle you were standing when you asked, and nothing in the number says which one you have.

There is a second trap in the same field. Illinois assesses residential property at a fraction of market value, roughly 10%, so 3,041 is not a $3,041 property and 1,303 is not a $1,303 one. The number is a step in a tax calculation, never a price.

I asked the same question seventeen hundred miles away. Parcel 3532803300, a house on Ridgegate Row in La Jolla, came back at 2,022,509.

That is a Proposition 13 factored base year value: what the property was worth when it last changed hands, grown by at most 2% a year since. For a house that last sold in the 1970s, that is a 1970s price compounded at 2%, which is not what a buyer would pay now and was never meant to be. Also not a market value. Also not comparable to the Illinois number in any direction.

Hand both numbers to an AI agent and ask which property is worth more. It will answer. It has no reason not to.

I built an Apify Actor that answers one question, "tell me about this parcel", across four US counties that publish that answer four completely different ways, and hands it to an agent through the Apify MCP (Model Context Protocol) Server. It parses no HTML anywhere, because there is no web page in the loop for any of the four: three publish APIs and the fourth publishes a 531 MB file. It is a router and a normalizer, which is a less exciting description than scraper, and a more accurate one.

Four counties is not a coverage claim, and I want that out of the way early. The US Census Bureau's 2024 estimates list 3,144 counties and county equivalents. Mine are four of them: 10.9 million people, 3.2% of the country, 0.13% of its counties. I picked them because each one forces a different access mode.

The caller is not a person

Every design decision below comes from one fact: the thing reading the answer is an agent, and an agent is not a person with a browser tab open.

A person asks about one county at a time. They read the answer sitting next to the query they typed, in a page that says which county they are looking at, and when something is missing they notice, because they were looking for it. Most of the context lives outside the response and it is free.

An agent asking four counties about one property gets back a flat list. Nothing in its situation supplies what the response leaves out. If a record does not say which county answered, then for that agent nothing did.

Three rules follow, and the rest of this article is mostly them being tested.

No bare numbers. Every amount in the output carries what it is a value of, and where in the process it was taken. Both, because they are two different axes: Florida publishes six figures for one parcel that differ by what is being valued (just value, land value, assessed school, assessed non-school, taxable school, taxable non-school), while Cook's three differ by when you asked, with the thing being valued held constant. A record that labels amounts by basis alone holds Florida and loses Cook. One that labels by stage alone does the reverse. So both ride on the amount itself, and there is no field anywhere in the record that an adapter could put an unlabeled number into.

Uncertainty is machine readable first. Anything the caller has to know to avoid being wrong is a flag from a fixed vocabulary, and only then a sentence.

A refusal comes back in the shape of a success. An agent can act on a structured refusal and can only give up on an error.

The idea that a record should explain itself is not new, and I am not going to pretend it is. What is worth writing about is enforcement. The whole of it is five lines in the record builder:

const unique = [...new Set(flags)].sort();
const unknown = unique.filter((f) => !(f in FLAG_NOTES));
if (unknown.length) throw new Error(`unknown flag(s): ${unknown.join(', ')}`);

const record = {
    /* the rest of the record */
    flags: unique,
    notes: unique.map((f) => FLAG_NOTES[f]),
};

FLAG_NOTES is the vocabulary, one note per flag, and it is the only place a note exists. A flag outside it throws while the record is being built, so a typo cannot ship as a warning that is silently absent, and the sentences are generated from the flags rather than written next to them, so the two cannot drift apart. The full file is src/record.js in the repository.

Four counties, four access modes

I picked the four counties so that no two of them could be reached the same way.

Cook, IL San Diego, CA Duval, FL Travis, TX
how it publishes Socrata open data portal public ArcGIS REST statewide program, all 67 counties bulk export, no API
one parcel costs 6 requests, issued in parallel 1 request 1 request, parcel id only 0 requests, local index
measured 0.9 to 1.3 s 0.7 to 1.4 s 0.4 to 15 s about 35 ms, off a local disk
freshness, August 2026 one day old, serves 2025 no signal of any kind serves 2025 serves 2026

The request count is the honest column. The three live figures are from one datacenter in Japan on 2026-08-13, five rounds each: Duval alone swung from 0.4 to 14.9 seconds inside that minute. A latency without a vantage point is a bare number.

Cook has the best open data program of the four and still needs six requests to describe one parcel. Location, values, owner and sales are four datasets joined on the fourteen-digit parcel number, which Illinois calls a PIN, and building characteristics are in a fifth. Issued serially those six requests take five seconds, or two if one connection is reused; issued in parallel they take about one second, and that difference decides whether Cook fits inside an agent's patience at all.

Travis inverts the entire table. The appraisal district publishes no endpoint that answers a question about one parcel, only the whole certified roll as a 531 MB archive, so the Actor ingests it once and answers from an index. Lookups come back in about 35 milliseconds, because nobody is being asked anything.

It is also the only one of the four that cannot be refreshed on demand, and in August it was the only one carrying the freshest assessment year. Travis certified its 2026 roll on 2026-07-18 and posted it four days later. Florida's statewide layer served assessment year 2025 when I probed it on 2026-08-02 and was still serving 2025 when I checked again on 2026-08-05.

So the fastest source is the only one that cannot be refreshed, and the county with no API had fresher data than the state program with the nice REST endpoint. Speed and currency are not the same axis, and an agent that reads a fast answer as a fresh one is wrong here specifically.

By November that order had changed: Florida's layer had moved to 2026, and so had Cook's values. The ranking is a measurement with a date on it, and without the date it is a bare number too.

That is why the router has to hide two things rather than one. Schema differences, obviously. But latency classes too, and it must not hide freshness, which is why as_of.basis is a controlled vocabulary with four values and one of them is unknown. San Diego's layer exposes editingInfo: null, and no date field in it says when the data was last updated. Unknown is the honest answer there, and it is worse than stale, because stale can at least be flagged as stale.

Wiring it into an agent

The Apify MCP Server exposes Actors to agents as tools. You need three things before this works: an Apify account, your own Actor deployed to it and an MCP-capable client. In Claude Code that is one command:

claude mcp add --transport http apify "https://mcp.apify.com?tools=actors,<username>/<actor-name>"

The ?tools= parameter is the part worth copying. It replaces the default tool set rather than extending it. Without it the server also loads documentation search and a web browsing Actor, which is context the agent pays for on every single turn. With it, the session gets the actors category and my own Actor, and nothing else.

One thing that cost me time, and it is in no error message. The client reads its configuration at startup, so adding a server does not affect the session that added it. Nothing reports this. The tools are simply not there, and it looks like the URL is wrong.

The open question I had going in was whether a private Actor is exposed as its own tool or only reachable through a generic call-by-name. It gets its own tool, carrying the full input schema: enums, defaults and the prefill example. I had kept the generic call-actor in the URL as insurance and did not need it for that.

The consequence took me a moment to appreciate. The input schema descriptions arrive in the tool definition, which means they are read by the model at the moment it chooses arguments. They are documentation for the agent, not decoration for the console. This sentence, from the jurisdiction field, is doing real work:

There is no auto-detection: resolving a county from an address is a separate problem, and guessing it wrong returns a confident answer about the wrong property.

It is a validation rule that cannot be validated, so it is written as a prompt instead, and it sits exactly where the wrong guess would otherwise happen. The input schema is a prompt as much as it is a schema.

A prompt with a budget, it turns out. In August, descriptions over 500 characters were cut mid-word; now they are cut at the last full sentence and marked [Description truncated], with the same 500 limit. I measured the number before I found it in the server's README, because nothing in the deploy points there. Two of my five were over, and the one offering a choice about publishing a person's name lost every word about what the choice does. Whatever changes a decision goes first now, and a test fails if it does not.

One caveat found the hard way, on the day I shipped a change. The tool definition my connected session held was a snapshot. I added an input field, redeployed, and the already-connected session still advertised the old four fields. Nothing errored. From the agent's side the field did not exist, so it kept calling the old shape and getting valid answers computed under the old default. The generic call-actor, the insurance I thought I had wasted, is what made the new field reachable before a reconnect.

The output side had none of that care. With no declared schema the platform tells an agent what an Actor returns by inferring it from recent runs, and mine came back as flags/0, flags/1, flags/2. Three flag fields, because that run had three flags. Declaring a dataset schema replaces the guess with the vocabulary in the dataset's metadata, though fetch-actor-details still infers, and writing one cost a failed run and found three places my own normalizer had drifted. That is worth knowing before you declare one: the platform validates every item on push and kills the Actor, which neither test suite could catch, because pushing is the only place a declaration and a record meet.

The console's Origin column reading MCP for the agent-driven runs, and CLI for the one deploy check I ran by hand.

What came back, and what came back instead

Here is the Cook parcel this article opened with, as the agent received it.

{
  "valuation": {
    "amounts": [
      { "basis": "il_fractional_assessed", "stage": "mailed",          "amount": 3041 },
      { "basis": "il_fractional_assessed", "stage": "certified",       "amount": 3041 },
      { "basis": "il_fractional_assessed", "stage": "board_of_review", "amount": 1303 }
    ],
    "headline_basis": "il_fractional_assessed",
    "headline_stage": "board_of_review"
  },
  "flags": ["parcel_not_current", "sale_price_nominal", "values_under_appeal"]
}

Nine amounts in the real record, three shown. headline_stage names which single figure to quote when only one can be shown, and values_under_appeal exists because an agent reading board_of_review otherwise has no way to know the other two stages say something else.

Then the flag I did not expect to be writing about. parcel_not_current: this parcel stopped existing after 2016. Cook's historical datasets answer for it anyway, with an owner and values, and only the current-year universe knows it is gone. Three consecutive runs returned the same confident decade-old answer.

Which is the opening problem again, one turn deeper. Every figure in that record is correct. None of them is an answer about a property that exists, and correct is not the same as being the answer to the question that was asked.

The second artifact is a partial answer that says how partial it is. Asking Duval for 1431 Riverplace Blvd, Jacksonville returns five records, each carrying:

{
  "result_set": { "matched": 241, "returned": 5, "envelope_degrees": 0.002 },
  "flags": ["address_resolved_to_building", "resolved_via_external_geocoder", "results_truncated"]
}

The address is a condominium tower and Florida publishes one centroid per parcel, so it is 241 parcels, one per unit. "241 matched, you are seeing 5" and "one of the sections failed to load" are different facts that need different reactions from the caller, which is why they are different flags rather than one partial_result.

The third artifact is a refusal, and refusals are the reason this contract exists. Travis, asked for a parcel on the platform, where no index ships:

{
  "result": "index_not_built",
  "jurisdiction": { "county": "Travis", "state": "TX", "fips": "48453" },
  "requested": { "lookup_by": "parcel_id", "query": "100008" },
  "source": { "mode": "bulk_index", "endpoints": [] },
  "reason": "This county publishes no endpoint that answers a question about one parcel, so answers come from an index built from the certified export. No index has been built yet, and the platform build ships none.",
  "remedy": "Clone the repository and run bin/build-travis-index.js. It fetches 129 MB of a 531 MB archive and takes under a minute."
}

That is not an exception and not an error string. It names who refused, what was asked, what was contacted (nobody, and the empty array says so rather than the field being absent), why, and what to do about it. An agent can act on remedy. It can only give up on a stack trace.

One distinction matters here: genuinely empty is not a refusal. A parcel id that does not exist in the county comes back as an empty list, because that is a true answer. Duval's address_not_geocoded is a refusal because the trip failed rather than the address being absent, and the record carries how far the search went, so the caller can tell "there is no such parcel" from "I could not look".

That distinction is only worth anything on parcels I did not choose. Mine were four, picked while writing the adapters, so after publishing I sampled out of each county's own list instead. The first 250 broke something: headline_stage, the label naming which figure to quote, said board of review on Cook parcels whose year carried only the mailed values, so 99 of 250 named an amount that was not there. The parcel this article opens with has all three, which is why four of my own choosing could not have shown it. Fixed, and the next 10,000 broke none of the nine checks. Then I fed 200 of their addresses back in, and one Duval road address answered with the unit inside the building, one record and nothing to say so: the guard watches the filter, not the set.

Five records returned, 241 matched, and the flags that say why.

What did not work first

Every rule above was bought with a mistake. Here they are in the order of how much each one changed the design.

I believed an error message five times

I rewrote the same filter five times, believing the message, before I accepted that my parameters had never been the problem. Filtering the statewide layer on an address returns HTTP 200 with {"error":{"code":400,"message":"Cannot perform query. Invalid query parameters."}} in the body, for a query whose parameters are demonstrably valid. It is deterministic: seven measurements across two dates fall between 55.5 and 58.5 seconds, with a 4.7 second control on the same connection. The real cause is an internal scan timeout across 10.8 million rows, reported as a client error.

Which is where it stops being a curiosity and starts being a design constraint. Asking the same filter for identifiers only returns all 398,063 parcels of one county in four seconds, and the same trick does nothing for an address: the service will spend 56 seconds failing to count the rows matching one street. So the response shape was a red herring. One predicate column is indexed, the other is not, and nothing published says which. The error body arrived in three different shapes across three days, which rules out matching on the message string as well.

The rule: success means the body carries the shape I asked for. Status codes and message strings are commentary. And a deterministic failure gets a different call shape, because an agent that retries this one spends three minutes of its own budget to hear the same thing.

The empty array that looked like my own mistake

The first thing I checked was my own filter, because an empty array is what a wrong filter looks like too. Summing the assessed total over the layer returns HTTP 200, the output field properly declared, and "features": []. The sum overflows the 32-bit integer the statistic is typed as. Binary search puts the boundary exactly: the first 1,793 parcels sum to 2,147,271,276 and answer, parcel 1,794 adds 627,300, and the row vanishes against a ceiling of 2,147,483,647. Nothing in that response is malformed. response.ok is true, there is no error key, the fields are populated, and a well-formed empty array is exactly what "no matching records" looks like. It took a control to convince me otherwise: count and max over the same 1,089,648 rows both answer in under two seconds, so the query was fine and the arithmetic was not.

What it changed: the classifier grew a fifth bucket, empty that should not be. The Actor now decides per call whether empty is a possible correct answer, because the caller cannot tell from the response, and an agent handed an empty list will report "no such parcel" with complete confidence.

My reconnaissance was wrong about Cook, and the tell was sitting there

I read the four obvious datasets, found no floor area, no year built, no bedroom count, and concluded that Cook does not publish building characteristics. The correct conclusion was "these four do not, so where is it". They are in a fifth dataset, and which fifth depends on whether the building is a house or a condominium. Travis repeated the trap in a completely different publishing model: the main file of the export carries no floor area either, and it is in two more files in the same archive.

What I take from it: a missing field is a question. The tell was structural and sitting in front of me: the contract promised a characteristics block and nothing was going to fill it, which is the same signal an agent gets when a section comes back null.

There is no envelope width that is correct

Around a geocoded point, plus or minus 22 meters found my reference house exactly, one candidate, no ambiguity. That width was not a guess, which is why I trusted it: it had just worked perfectly on a detached house. Around a condominium tower it returned zero. Widening to 55 meters returned four units of a different building, as a clean success with nothing in it to say so. San Diego breaks the same route in the opposite direction: one point returned 90 parcels across three street names and $36.9 million of combined value, in 1.5 seconds, no flag and no error, because condominiums, possessory interests and mobile homes are all stacked on the parent parcel's polygon.

What the contract says now: a spatial hit is a candidate set, and it stays one until address attributes narrow it. If several candidates survive, the caller is told the address named a building.

493,246 properties do not fit in a 4 GB heap

The data is small. The objects around it are not, at roughly 8 KB of overhead each once owners, addresses and values are nested. A bigger heap is a monthly bill on this platform, so I went looking for the property that would make one unnecessary, and found that the export happens to be sorted by property id, which the county's own layout spec never mentions. A property is therefore complete the moment a different id appears, and can be written out and forgotten.

What shipped with it: a design leaning on an undocumented property carries its own check. The builder counts out-of-order identifiers instead of trusting the ordering, zero across 493,324 records, and reports that count in the index manifest, so the day it stops being true the output says so.

One thing that has never been tested

Travis supplements are a change log, with add, modify and delete actions applied in order. The certified file I built the index from has supplement number 0 and an empty action on every one of its 493,324 records, so the code handling those actions has never seen a supplement. It is written from a document.

Stated, not implied: untested code is a known limitation and belongs in the open, on the same discipline as the flags. What the caller has to know to avoid being wrong gets said out loud, and that includes what the author has not managed to verify yet.

The run log. Container pull, SDK boot, then the lookup.

The two things only the agent found

Everything above came out of the reconnaissance or out of writing the adapters. Two things came out of handing the finished Actor to an agent and reading what came back, and neither is about a county.

The refusal path had never been normalized, and nobody had noticed, because humans read refusals

The success path had one constructor and a validated vocabulary from the first commit. That is why four adapters written weeks apart produce identical record shapes. Refusals were object literals at five separate call sites, and they had drifted. Three of the five did not name the county at all. The endpoint appeared under three different key names across the five. The one refusal that did name its county had the FIPS code typed into the adapter by hand instead of read from the jurisdiction table.

None of that is visible while the person reading the output is the person who typed the query. You know which county you asked, because you asked one, and it is on your screen. An agent asking four counties about one property gets a flat list back, and three of five possible refusals in it cannot say who refused.

That is the failure the whole contract exists to prevent, sitting on the one path the contract never covered. The rule that every answer names its source had simply never been applied to refusals, because I had never read one from outside.

Refusals now go through one constructor, in the same src/record.js, and it enforces exactly what the success path had enforced all along:

if (!REFUSAL_CODES.has(result)) throw new Error(`unknown refusal result: ${result}`);
if (!reason) throw new Error(`refusal ${result} has no reason`);

Two lines, and they are two lines I could have written on day one. I redeployed and reran the same lookups over MCP: the refusals came back in one shape, and the Cook success record came back with the same 42 fields as before, so the fix left alone what it was meant to leave alone.

The number the platform reports is mostly not the county

The console and the MCP response both say the Cook lookup took 2.81 seconds. The Actor's own log says the lookup took 275 milliseconds. About 2.1 seconds of that run was container pull and SDK boot before the first byte left for Illinois, and the same lookup rerun in November spent about 3.5 seconds there and answered in 213 ms.

The run time and the lookup time are close enough in magnitude to be mistaken for each other, and the routing table in my own contract measures counties while anything measured through a run measures the platform as well. Travis shows it worst: the August Travis run took 2.15 seconds and returned no data at all, because the platform image ships no index.

What it refuses to do

Four limits, each one a decision rather than a gap.

It will not guess the county from an address. The jurisdiction is a required enum with no auto-detect option, though the console preselects San Diego, which I would not do again: a default is a guess too. Resolving an address to a county is a separate problem with its own failure modes, and I would rather refuse the lookup than fold that problem silently into this one. This is less friendly than the alternative, on purpose.

Public documented endpoints only. Travis publishes bulk files and no documented API, and behind its vendor property search there is clearly a backend; the county's own page even links to a staging host for it. I found that, wrote it down, and did not touch it. An undocumented internal endpoint can change without notice, and a staging host is plainly not meant for public traffic. That decision costs coverage, and it is the entire reason Travis is a 531 MB download instead of a portal call.

Tax amounts are out of scope. In all four jurisdictions the amount owed belongs to a treasurer or a collector, a different agency from the assessor. "Property tax lookup" is exactly what a caller will assume it returns, so the Actor says so rather than silently omitting it.

Owner names, where the publishers disagree, are withheld by default. San Diego's assessor served me an owner name on every parcel I queried, unauthenticated, on 2026-08-02 and again on 2026-08-05. The joint city and county GIS agency states that California AB1785 bars it from publishing owner name and address in any publicly accessible online location. Both statements are current, and it is not this Actor's job to settle which one governs.

It does not settle it. It stops shipping the field by default, and the record says what it did and how to change it. Ask for the name explicitly and it comes back carrying a different flag, saying its publication is disputed, so the fact travels with the data instead of ending at the first hop.

Availability is not permission. Shipping whatever an endpoint hands over is not a neutral default either: it picks the same side of that disagreement, silently.

The related case is where the source itself marks a record confidential, which Travis's export can do per owner. There the answer is "this parcel exists and the person is withheld", never "not found", and the Actor does not reconstruct a suppressed owner by joining another source.

What I would keep

Three things generalize past this Actor.

The input schema is a prompt. Its field descriptions are read by the model choosing the arguments, so they are the cheapest place in the whole system to prevent a wrong call. Write them for a reader who has never seen a parcel id, and fit that in 500 characters.

A refusal is a record. Anything an agent can receive has to be as structured as the thing you designed on purpose. And the path you never read yourself is the path that drifts, which means the question to ask about any agent-facing output is not "is this correct" but "who reads this, and what do they already know that the record does not say".

The value is in what the record refuses to flatten: three stages of one year, five rungs of one ladder, a clamp that looks like a measurement, a parcel that stopped existing a decade ago.

Two things I would do differently. I would write the refusal constructor before the fourth adapter rather than after an agent read its output, because the fix took twenty minutes and the drift had been shipping for four versions. And I would decide where the Travis index lives before building it locally: answering index_not_built with the command to run is honest, and it is also a decision I deferred by shipping a message about it.

The Actor is on GitHub: actor-us-tax-county-scraper. Four adapters, the record and refusal constructors, 96 unit tests, 26 live ones against the real counties, which is how I learn when one of them changes something, and the sweep that draws them. It also runs from the Apify Store without cloning anything, for every county but Travis, which answers index_not_built there.

If you are pointing an agent at a source that answers more than one way, tell me what your record refuses to flatten.

About the author.

Mikhail Koviazin is a backend engineer working on data extraction. In 2017 he built Google Maps crawlers on Apifier, as Apify was then called. Between 2020 and 2022 he built a scraping layer on top of Apify SDK v1, the codebase that later became Crawlee, running more than 5 million products a day across 1000+ sites, patching the SDK locally where its public interface did not expose what he needed. He now builds Actors that AI agents call directly.

articles.title: I built a private, offline AI chat you can run with one command: npx unmuzzled
articles.description: A local LLM chat app built on llama.cpp, Node and a hand-built web UI, plus what it took to make localhost secure and ship the same model on Android.
articles.body_html:
Most AI chat apps send every prompt to someone else's servers. I wanted the opposite: a chat app where the model runs on my hardware, works offline, and takes one command to start.

npx unmuzzled

That's Unmuzzled. It's open source (MIT), and this post covers how it works and the problems I didn't expect.

A real run on my laptop. The reasoning streams first, then the answer. Generation is sped up 8×; the real speed (1.7 tok/s) is shown at the end.

What it does

  • Opens a chat UI in your browser. On first run, a setup screen shows the model, its size, your RAM and free disk, and downloads nothing until you click Download (with pause and resume).
  • Runs the model locally through llama.cpp via node-llama-cpp, using Vulkan, CUDA or Metal when available.
  • Streams answers with Markdown and syntax highlighting, and shows the model's reasoning live in a collapsible, timed panel.
  • Supports editing, regenerating and searchable history. Chats are stored only in your browser.
  • Works with any GGUF model: npx unmuzzled --model ./your-model.gguf.

Why it's different

There are great local-AI tools already. Most of them assume you're comfortable with a terminal, model formats and config files. Unmuzzled is built for the person who just wants a private AI that works:

  • Nothing to set up. No Python, Docker or config files. One command on desktop, one tap on Android. The app checks your RAM and disk and fetches the right file; you never need to know what "Q4_K_M GGUF" means.
  • Private by design. The model runs on your device. After the one-time download it works in airplane mode, and there is no account, telemetry or server.
  • No refusal filters. The default model has had its refusal training removed (details below), so it answers questions mainstream assistants decline. That's useful for research, security work and fiction, and it means the judgement is yours.
  • Same experience everywhere. The desktop and Android apps share the same design, the same model and the same reasoning view.

The model

The default is a 9B model with an interesting family tree:

  1. Qwen3.5-9B, the base model
  2. Jackrong/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Qwen3.5-9B, fine-tuned on ~250k reasoning samples generated by DeepSeek-V4-Pro
  3. xtools-at/…-UNCENSORED-heretic, with refusal behaviour removed using Heretic
  4. mradermacher/…-i1-GGUF, quantised to Q4_K_M (5.63 GB)

Every step is Apache-2.0. Despite the name, it is not DeepSeek's model; it's a small Qwen model trained to imitate DeepSeek's reasoning style. Unmuzzled doesn't redistribute the weights; they download straight from Hugging Face.

Because refusal training has been removed, it answers things other assistants decline, and like any LLM it can be confidently wrong. The README has a responsible-use section, and any model with safety training intact works too.

How it works

The whole thing is deliberately small: no framework and no build step on the desktop side.

bin/unmuzzled.js   CLI: arguments, setup state, model download, startup
src/server.js      HTTP server, static files, streaming chat API (SSE)
src/engine.js      node-llama-cpp wrapper, reasoning/answer separation
src/models.js      model catalog, download with pause/resume
public/            the interface: plain HTML, CSS and ES modules

Streaming. The browser POSTs the conversation to /api/chat, and the server streams Server-Sent Events: thought chunks, text chunks, and a final done event with token count and tokens/second. node-llama-cpp separates the model's reasoning into segments; for templates that don't, a small state machine splits <think>…</think> out of the raw stream, including tags that arrive split across chunks.

The UI. I wanted it to look like a carefully made desktop tool rather than a template: warm neutrals, one muted accent, IBM Plex Sans and Mono served locally (so it works offline), hand-drawn icons, and no gradients or glow. Model output is untrusted, so raw HTML is escaped and remote images are never fetched.

The part I didn't expect: localhost security

A local AI server feels private, but any website you visit can try to talk to 127.0.0.1. Two attacks matter:

  • CSRF-style requests. A page can fire a text/plain POST at your local server without a CORS preflight. Unmuzzled requires application/json, which forces a preflight the server never approves.
  • DNS rebinding. A malicious domain can resolve to 127.0.0.1 after the page loads, making the browser treat your local server as same-origin. Unmuzzled rejects any request whose Host header isn't a local name.

The same guard protects the setup endpoints, so no website can start a 5 GB download on your machine.

Honest numbers

On my laptop (Intel i5-1135G7, Iris Xe integrated graphics via Vulkan, 16 GB RAM), the 9B model runs at about 2 tokens/second (1.7–2.7 across my runs) after a ~40–50 second load. "Offline" doesn't mean "fast"; hardware is the whole story. A discrete GPU or an Apple Silicon Mac is many times faster. Reasoning models also generate their thinking before the answer, which adds to wait time on slow hardware.

Shipping it on Android

The Android app (beta) runs the same uncensored model on the phone itself. It's not a thin client for a server or your laptop; once the model is downloaded, the phone needs no network at all.

What using it looks like:

  1. Open the app. It checks your phone's memory and free storage and tells you whether the 9B model will fit (it needs about 12 GB of RAM, which current flagships have).
  2. Tap Download. The 5.6 GB model downloads with a progress bar, speed and time left. You can pause it, and if you leave the app it saves its place and resumes when you come back. The screen stays on until it's done.
  3. Chat. Replies stream in with Markdown and a collapsible reasoning panel. A Think toggle in the composer switches between deep reasoning and instant answers.

Already have a GGUF file? "I already have a .gguf file" imports it from the phone's storage instead. Chats, settings and the model live only on the device, and there's no sign-in.

Under the hood it's React Native (Expo) with llama.rn. It ships llama.cpp builds tuned for modern ARM cores (dotprod/i8mm) and optional OpenCL offload on Adreno GPUs. Download the APK (beta). Open it on the phone and allow installs from that source when asked.

Building it on Windows was its own adventure:

  • Gradle couldn't download anything until I forced Java onto IPv4. The network's IPv6 was broken, and Java tried it first.
  • A Markdown library imported Node's built-in punycode, which doesn't exist in React Native, so I installed the standalone package.
  • Windows' 260-character path limit broke the native build: one library's generated C++ paths reached 297 characters, and Android's bundled Ninja 1.10 can't use long paths. I replaced the library with a 30-line Kotlin module that reads the system bar insets directly.

The app goes on GitHub Releases rather than Google Play. An app built around an uncensored model doesn't fit Play's AI-content policy, and side-loading an open-source APK is a well-trodden path.

Try it 

npx unmuzzled                         # setup screen, then chat
npx unmuzzled --model ./model.gguf    # bring your own model
  • GitHub: https://github.com/rahulagarwal18/unmuzzled
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/unmuzzled

If you run it, I'd love to know your tokens/second and hardware. Issues and PRs are welcome.
